recommendations.text: The fps is in its production ramp. Safety and quality come before rate. Gate each production step on the KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training), never on the calendar. Bring in-service reliability and the durability of both engine sources (CFM and the Joint Venture engine) to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting. That committee brings propulsion expertise to that review. Report any quality, FAA or supply problem to us as a live problem.

Engine supply. The enabler is met at two sources, CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, not the three planned in 2035, because the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one source. Keep both sources supplied and hot. Watch CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket. Report the supplier-shortages KPI, engines first. Keep development and support terms on risk-share or cost-plus, never fixed price.

Capital allocation, answering the CEO's 2035 recommendation:
- The 2036 cash peak is past. Net debt has stayed at the historical level since 2029 in the base case and 2030 in the stress case. By our computation from the brief, stress-case free cash flow runs about $15.2B (2040), $16.4B (2045) and $17.2B (2050).
- Any dividend or buyback is reserved to this Board, and the tracker's surplus-to-owners rule does not decide it for us. We are open to a proposal.
- Bring it with the rating view and the stress-case net-debt path. Size it so net debt stays at or below the historical level in the stress case, with a liquidity cushion kept through the fps ramp and any 2050 widebody decision.
- Keep returns well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow.
- No new equity.

Public statement and objectives:
- Give no new dates, and do not answer Airbus's calendar.
- Reaffirm safety, quality, KPI-gated production, two engine sources and debt first.
- Accept plainly that no order this round moves narrowbody share: incumbency was missed in 2040 (38%), and the 50/50 split stays out of reach (47% in 2050). Pay no objective premium for either.
- Debt repair and the engine enabler are met in both plans.

- Base free cash flow: $19.8B (2040), $20.9B (2045), $21.8B (2050).
- Stress case, my reading: about $15.2B, $16.4B and $17.2B. Malave should confirm.

- fps_engine_code: null. The code has been fixed since EIS.
- rate_737: hold.
- re787: hold.

**Why hold.** This is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / +0.34.

**Off the board:**

- durability reviews of both engine sources for the Aerospace Safety Committee;
- supplier health, engines first;
- 787 growth from Charleston;
- a measured capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, sized on the stress case.

tests.name: Capital allocation for the Board's reserved decision (CEO ask 6; advice)

tests.numbers:
Proposal (inference; my record has no returns history):
- Reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.4x by 2045 stress FCF of $16.35B.
- Add a flexible buyback of $0-5B a year, paced on actual FCF.
- Cap the two together at $8B a year: 49% of 2045 stress FCF and 38% of base FCF ($20.94B).

That covers a 2050 widebody bill of $5B many times over. Revolvers stay undrawn and there is no new equity. The Board revisits the cap at the 2050 review, with upside held back.
What breaks it: FCF more than about 51% below the stress case (62% below base). With the buyback flexed to zero, the dividend holds unless FCF falls about 82% below stress.
Rating view: we were Baa3 with a negative outlook in January 2025. On these metrics I read us as solidly investment grade: net debt at the 2010-18 level since 2029-30, stress FCF of $15-17B, no added debt. The brief carries no rating and the analyst file has no rating thresholds, so this is inference, to be confirmed against the agencies' view.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Four things would change my view.
(1) Re-engine: a later grid, the 2050 review at the earliest and only if the A350 has not been re-engined, that shows the 787 Re-engine clearing epsilon ($1B) in the expected column with no column below -$1B. Nothing on this grid does: even at 0% weight on S2 its +0.30 sits inside epsilon, and hold wins on expectation at any S2 weight above 19.2%.
(2) Returns: free cash flow running more than about half below the stress case, under $8B against $16.35B in 2045. I would then shrink the buyback to zero first. The about-$3B dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 82% below stress.
(3) Live problem: Pope reporting a live quality, FAA or supply problem on the fps ramp, or on either engine source. I would hold harder and defer the buyback until it is closed.
(4) Rating: an agency view below solidly investment grade. That would cut returns to the dividend only until it is restored.
No binding veto applies this round, since the brief has no risk-case column. If the GM or Board ruled that S2 is the risk case, both rows still pass: A at +0.34, and B at -0.92 against a -1.66 floor.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I read the rule as you do. The brief labels no risk case, so there is no slip leg and I hold no veto. For the Board, I ran S2 as if it were the risk case: the floor is +0.34 less $2.00B, or -1.66. Do Nothing sits at +0.34 and the Re-engine row at -0.92, $0.74B above the floor. Both pass, as advice.

The business case decides, and it does not clear. The Re-engine adds +0.30 in S1, inside epsilon, and gives up $1.26B in S2. Cash is not the constraint: $5B over 2045-49 peaks at $1.35B in 2048 and leaves stress free cash flow near $15.9B. I see no finance reason to open a second development for that trade. Hold wins at any S2 weight above 19%; I plan on about half.

I confirm your stress read: $15.2B, $16.35B and $17.2B (2040, 2045, 2050). Net debt holds at $0.0B at every checkpoint, base and stress, in both rows; the objective cell rebuilds as 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B).

On returns, my proposal for the Board: reinstate a common dividend of about $3B and add a flexible buyback, together capped at $8B a year, under half of stress free cash flow. Retain the rest until liquidity reaches about $15B, revolvers undrawn, no new equity.

This baseline lets us meet it and potentially beat it, barring free cash flow more than half below the stress case. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet stays first.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery, plan A, Do Nothing (fps hold + 787 hold). Basis: my record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference
tests.threshold: Can the plan be delivered as stated? The brief labels no risk-case column (S1: rivals hold; S2: Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine), so I read each plan's worst column and say how much of its value depends on a nominal date.
tests.numbers: A's worst column is S2, at +0.34. All of A's value comes from an fps that has been in service since 2040; none of it depends on a future date. Delay Tactics can no longer be ordered, because the fps is in service. Observed narrowbody share was 38/39/40/41/42% over 2040-44. That is the board's no-delay path: NGSA entered service in 2037 and the fps in 2040, a 3-year lead, so the long-run split is 47/53. Under Delay Tactics the record would show 5 pp less, 33-37% (my inference from rules.md). The supply chain and workforce therefore held through EIS. The $0.32B gap between S1 and S2 (+0.66 to +0.34) comes from an Airbus move, not from our delivery.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery, plan B, 787 Re-engine launched in 2045 for EIS 2050. Basis: my record [BX-1331] by inference; the slip prior is doctrine (profile.md §3)
tests.threshold: EIS can be delivered as stated, with headroom against doctrine's slip prior for a major derivative (+1 to +4 years, central +2). No risk case is labelled, so I read the worst column.
tests.numbers: B's worst column is S2, at -0.92, which is $1.26B below A. The board's 5-year clock (launch 2045, EIS 2050) is the nominal date and carries no headroom against our +1 to +4-year prior. Each $1B at 2050 is worth $0.091B of PV at 2026 (10.5% over 24 years). A 2-year slip cuts S1's +0.30 to about +0.25 from discounting alone, before any cost growth. About $3.3B of cost growth at EIS, 66% of the $5B bill, erases it entirely. All of the +0.30 also depends on Airbus not re-engining the A350. This is advice, not a veto.

tests.name: fps production ramp against the KPIs (CEO ask 2). Basis: doctrine [B-2221, B-2351, B-2283, BX-1259, BX-1291], not my record
tests.threshold: Rate steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, each gated on the six FAA-agreed KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training, ticketing), with no live quality, FAA or supply problem.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity, both rows (CEO ask 3). Basis: doctrine [B-0341, B-0373], H4; arithmetic from dashboard_game.md §2
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap by at most 2 years. Strain is $3B × overlap ÷ 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS. One major development at a time.
tests.numbers: The fps development ran 2033-40 and a 2045 Re-engine would run 2045-50, so the overlap is 0 years and strain is $0 on both A and B. H4 does not strike B. Can engineering carry a widebody development beside the fps ramp and in-service support? Yes, on doctrine. The fps development is finished, so the Re-engine would be the only major development [B-0341]. Derivative R&D starts 3-4 years before delivery and peaks 1-2 years before it [B-0373]: about 2046-47 and 2048-49 here, a decade after the fps engineering peak in 2038-39. Engineering capacity does not bind this round; the business case does.

tests.name: Re-engine engine readiness by a 2050 EIS, concurrency, and invest or partner (CEO ask 5). Basis: inference on the public record; doctrine's engine choice in profile.md §6
tests.threshold: An engine ready by EIS with margin. No production ahead of a mature, certifiable design. Invest where Boeing owns the IP.
tests.numbers: GE would supply it. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS, and doctrine's default is GE. Rolls-Royce has no widebody engine move under way and says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. An UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, a year after EIS. So a 2050 Re-engine would fly one source, GE, where the 787 flies two today (GE and Rolls-Royce [B-0940]) (inference). Concurrency: the engine would not pace the programme, unlike the GE9X on the 777X [B-1597]. We avoid concurrency only if production waits for a mature design certified with the FAA [BX-1263], which is why the date needs headroom (plan B, above). Invest or partner: invest, because the 787 airframe IP is ours [BX-1330]. The engine maker comes in on risk-share or cost-plus terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

tests.name: Supplier readiness, engines first (CEO ask 4). Basis: doctrine [B-2308, B-1449, BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043, BX-1264, BX-1325, BX-1298], not my record
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain problem, and the supplier-shortages KPI not flagged. At least two engine sources on the fps. Fragile suppliers kept funded and hot.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no supply-chain problem. The fps flies CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine: two sources in 2045 and 2050, with three makers in the market.

CFM capacity:
- Observed narrowbody engine shares for 2040-44 are CFM 27.0%, P&W 36.5% and RR 36.5%. Of 4,000 engines a year, that is about 1,080, 1,460 and 1,460.

Joint Venture engine:

Fragility: the enabler sits at exactly two sources, because the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one. A durability problem on the Joint Venture engine would leave the fps on CFM alone.

LEAP-1B: the brief gives no 737 MAX and fps mix. LEAP-1B remains the sole source for any MAX still built and for the installed fleet's aftermarket [B-1449].

Keep hot: CFM on the fps, the Joint Venture engine, LEAP-1B, and any supplier flagged on shortages. The ladder is embed, buffer, keep above rate, requalify, fund, acquire [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043].

Each aircraft is worth $180M, so 787 revenue is $18.0B (derived from the 2026 row: $56.4B less 800 × $48M). Charleston growth is therefore unpriced. Plan A: base free cash flow is $19.83B (2040), $20.94B (2045) and $21.83B (2050). The implied consensus base is about $13.78B, so the stress base (two-thirds) is $9.18B. Plan B:
- The Re-engine's $5B is spent over 2045-49, about $1B a year if spread evenly (the curve shape is Malave's). At the tracker's 79%, that takes $0.79B a year of free cash flow, $3.95B in total.

ops.memo:
My record is Global Services. Delivery, IP and cash conversion are my record, applied by inference. KPIs, strain and suppliers run on Boeing's operations doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The fps has five years in service. Share has climbed a point a year, 38% to 42%, with no Delay Tactics loss. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. My KPI veto has nothing to bind: the rate is hold only.

Second, the ramp. Deliveries go from 63 a month in 2040 to 78 in 2049: three steps of 5 in nine years, a sixth of doctrine's fastest tempo. The six KPIs are not in the brief as numbers. I table them, with in-service reliability, at the Aerospace Safety Committee.

Third, engines. We sit at exactly two sources. If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on one. Keep CFM, the Joint Venture engine and LEAP-1B funded and hot.

Fourth, the Re-engine. Strain is $0. But only GE is ready for 2050; Rolls-Royce would be 2051 at the earliest, so the 787 would drop from two engine sources to one. The five-year clock has no headroom against our slip prior. Each $1B at 2050 is $0.09B of PV today; $3.3B of cost growth erases the +0.30; in S2 it is still $5B behind after twenty years.

And finally, cash. Hold keeps stress free cash flow at $16.3B in 2045; the Re-engine takes $0.79B a year of it.

Orders: all hold, code null.

other_moves.move: KPI-gated fps production ramp, with every step reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee
other_moves.detail:
fps production steps up in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart. Each step is gated on the FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283].

On the brief, deliveries go from 760 (2040) to 860 (2045) and 940 (2049): three steps of 5 in nine years, a sixth of doctrine's fastest tempo.

Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].

other_moves.move: In-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources
other_moves.detail:
CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting [BX-1298].

The fps is fitted CFM + P&W + RR, but the Joint Venture engine counts as one source. That leaves us at exactly two sources. If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone. Any durability finding is a live problem, and I would then want a third source.

CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325]. It has eased: CFM's narrowbody share is 27% in 2040-44 against 76% before 2037, while the fps needs about 1,720 engines in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049.

other_moves.move: Supplier health, engines first: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated
other_moves.detail: We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336]. It loads the factory, not engineering (strain $0), and it is our widebody answer in place of a second development: doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. The board does not price it.

other_moves.move: Capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, sized on the stress case
other_moves.detail:
Malave's sizing, which I endorse. This is inference: neither of us has a record on returns.

The proposal:
- Reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.4x by 2045 stress free cash flow of $16.35B.
- Add a flexible buyback of $0-5B a year, paced on actual free cash flow.
- Cap the two together at $8B a year: 49% of 2045 stress free cash flow and 38% of base ($20.94B). That is well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164].
- Retain about $8.4-9.2B a year under stress for 2045-49. That builds liquidity of about $44B by end-2049, enough to carry a 2050 widebody bill of $5B many times over.

The safeguards:
- Net debt stays at $0 at every checkpoint, base and stress.
- The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn, with no new equity.
- Supplier funding comes first.
- The buyback goes to zero first if free cash flow runs more than about half below the stress case, or if Pope reports a live problem.
- The dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 82% below stress.

Rating view (Malave, inference): solidly investment grade on these metrics [BX-1305], to be confirmed against the agencies before the Board decides.

The Board revisits the cap at the 2050 review. Nothing is announced before the Board decides.

other_moves.move: Widebody review in 2050, held only if the A350 has not been re-engined
No fixed-price development; no new dates
other_moves.detail: All development and support with suppliers stays on cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. We give no programme date before the data supports it [BX-1268, B-2315], and we blame no one, the FAA included [BX-1323].

decision.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for five years now, so let me tell you plainly where it stands. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Every step up in production is gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. We review how both engines are doing in service, every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development this year. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs allow. We'd rather do less and do it better. When there's a business case for the next step on the widebody, we'll bring it, and not before.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it stayed there through the heaviest spending years. Debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** Every order is at its default:
- fps: hold;
- fps_engine_code: null;
- rate_737: hold;
- re787: hold.

That is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 in S1 and +0.34 in S2. No order goes to the Board as a change.

**How the team rule ran (teams.md §9)**

1. *Malave's buffer test.* The brief labels no risk-case column. Malave and I read the rule the same way: there is no slip leg this round, the test is not applicable, and no binding veto stands.
   - For the Board, he ran S2 as if it were the risk case. The floor is +0.34 - 2.00 = -1.66.
   - Do Nothing passes at +0.34. The Re-engine row passes at -0.92, $0.74B clear.
   - This is advice only.
2. *KPI doctrine veto (Pope's seat).* It is moot. rate_737 is hold only, since the Rate Increase was a 2030-only lever. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem.
3. *My decision.* The only live choice is the 787 Re-engine.

**The 787 Re-engine against hold**

Its item value is +0.30 in S1 and -1.26 in S2.
- **Doing less, better [BX-1239].** +0.30 is inside ε ($1B), so the plan with less to execute wins.
- **Doctrine's own rule.** A Re-engine needs a gain above ε, and the A350 must not have re-engined. The first condition fails. This is doctrine (dashboard_game.md §6; profile §6), not my record.
- **Higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].** Hold's worst column is +0.34; the Re-engine's is -0.92.
- **Expectation.** Hold wins at any S2 weight above 19.2% (0.30 / 1.56). At 50% it leads by $0.48B (+0.50 against +0.02).
- **The Board.** It would veto a launch on both of its tests:
  - +0.30 is below its $1B launch test;
  - -1.26 in S2 breaches its -$1B downside limit.
- **Option value.** If Airbus re-engines the A350 now, H3 closes the widebody and hold is right by $1.26B. If it does not, the case comes back in 2050 as a review.

Cash does not decide it. Malave shows the $5B is fundable: it peaks at $1.35B in 2048, and stress free cash flow stays at or above about $15.6B. Value decides it.

Pope adds two points, both advice:
- the 5-year clock has no headroom against our +1 to +4-year slip prior, and $3.3B of cost growth would erase the S1 gain;
- only GE is ready for a 2050 EIS, so the 787 would drop from two engine sources to one.

Both point the same way.

**Expected column: S2, narrowly.** Airbus tied its A350 priority to "until the new aircraft enters service". NGSA has been in service since 2037, and doctrine expects an A350 Re-engine attempt (profile §7, doctrine, not my record).

S1 is close behind, because Rolls-Royce says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. Malave plans on about 50%.

I hold no Airbus evidence of my own (Low). Hold is the right order in either column, so the call on the column changes only the premium log.

**Rulings on the hard rules**
- **H1 and H3, first half:** ruled in 2030, spent, not in force.
- **H2:** cannot bind.
- **H3, second half:** not fired, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- **H4:** a 2045 Re-engine (development 2045-50) would overlap the fps development (2033-40) by 0 years, so strain is $0.
- **H5:** nothing to cancel.

final.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for five years now, so let me tell you plainly where it stands. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Every step up in production is gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. We review how both engines are doing in service, every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development this year. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs allow. We'd rather do less and do it better. When there's a business case for the next step on the widebody, we'll bring it, and not before.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it stayed there through the heaviest spending years. Debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.

frame.situation:
BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only)
- fps was launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and has been in service since 2040. It flies code 7, with CFM certifying first. Boeing says it develops on cost-plus and risk-share terms, never fixed price.
- Boeing's last statement put debt first through its fps cash peak in 2036-37. That peak is now past.
- It puts 737 MAX and 787 customers first and will "keep growing the 787 out of the capacity we've built in Charleston". That reads as rate on today's 787, not a new engine.
- No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record. The GEnx upgrade has served the 787 since 2033, and CFM/GE's widebody engine share moved from 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042.

ENGINE MAKERS
- P&W and Rolls-Royce both committed in 2035, so the Joint Venture formed. GTF2 Solo and UltraFan NB Solo folded into it, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.
- CFM: the ducted engine has been ready since 2036 and the Embraer partnership since 2037. RISE stays funded as technology, with no date.
- Rolls-Royce: "Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody." It is improving Trent time on wing inside its existing budget. Today it is the A350's only engine source [A-0253].

PROBLEMS REPORTED
The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality event and no technology or engine slip. Our narrowbody deliveries are falling from 1,260 (2039) to 1,140 (2045). That is the board's share mechanics after fps entered service, not a supply event.

OUR POSITION
- NGSA has been in service since 2037. On code 7 it is fitted with CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (2 sources). The code can no longer change.
- If nobody moves, ΔPV is +23.37 (yield 115.58%): narrowbody operating profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 (booked at the 2037 EIS), debt penalty -0.53.
- Grid:
  - Hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). A 787 Re-engine costs the hold plan only $0.11B.
  - A350 Re-engine: +24.26 (S1) / +22.76 (S2).
  - The item is +0.89 / -0.50 and breaks even at a 64% chance of S2.
- No programme cash runs in 2045-2049 on hold. The A350 Re-engine would add $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year, 19% of the $5.2B line.

OBJECTIVE STATUS (scored by the GM; it never changes the payoff)
- Defend 60/40: NOT met. Narrowbody share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050. No option this round reaches it, because the A350 is widebody.
- Protect the A320 family: met at 60% before NGSA's EIS.
- Enabler: met in both plans. NGSA has 2 sources (CFM + the Joint Venture engine) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and 3 narrowbody makers (CFM, P&W, RR) are in the market in 2045 and 2050.

THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE (risk-averse, 4 of 5)
- It will approve either a hold or an A350 Re-engine launch that properly clears the ExCo's own tests, with S1 named as the expected column.
- It will veto a launch that goes through over a standing soft veto, a launch carried by an override, a launch Wagner fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and a launch where S2 is named as the expected column.

- Expected column: S1 (rivals hold), at about 70%. Boeing's stated priority is current 787 and 737 MAX stability, the GEnx upgrade already serves the 787, and Rolls-Royce says it plans no new widebody programme.
- S2 is more plausible than in 2035 because fps spending is past. I put it at about 30% (range 25-35%). It is the worst plausible column.
- Boeing's moves do not set our clock.

What we forgo. +0.89 in S1, about +0.47 weighted. A 2050 return enters service in 2055, with six counted years instead of eleven, each discounted five years more: under $0.61B on today's mechanics (inference). I do not count on it.

For the Board's twice-yearly safety review, what the record shows is thin:

(b) A320neo GTF fleet: P&W states that Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the GTF fleet, charged. It reviews pacing parts weekly so that Joint Venture work takes no parts or engineers from that insertion. No completion figure is on record.

- The NB market is flat at 2,000 a year.

- No engine slip is on record: CFM ducted ready 2036, Joint Venture engine ready 2036, CFM-Embraer 2037.

Our own-supply moves (work packages, titanium, rare earths) stay confined to our own ramp. The A350 Re-engine adds no concurrency (0 years of overlap).

tests.name: (4) Ramp shield: A320neo and NGSA, both plans
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open ramp commitment; a disciplined and controlled ramp. Passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.

tests.name: (5) Engineering capacity and rule 6: A350 Re-engine launched 2045 (EIS 2050)
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round (red line, rule 6).
tests.numbers:
- NGSA development: 2030-2036 (spending ended 2036, EIS 2037).
- A350 Re-engine development: 2045-2049, EIS 2050.
- Overlap: 0 years. Strain: $3B x 0/5 = $0.
- The NGSA engineering teams have been free for 9 years.
- One launch only: the A220-500 stays a study with no launch cash, so rule 6 holds.
- Rule 3, checked though not mine to enforce: no 787 Re-engine is on the public record.

tests.name: (6) A350F and Spirit absorption; A350 airframe production readiness for EIS 2050
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed (game proxy: round 2 at the earliest)
tests.numbers: 2045 is round 3. The A350F entered its industrial phase in 2025 and the Spirit A350 packages came in from 2026, so they have had about 20 years to be absorbed. The A350 line has delivered a steady 70 a year (41.2% of 170) since 2026, with no production event on record. The airframe side is ready for a 2050 EIS. The engine side is test 7.

tests.name: (7) A350 Re-engine engine readiness: a committed engine source by EIS 2050
tests.threshold: (Inference.) A named, committed engine maker with an engine ready by the Re-engine's EIS, on the record before the vote. Sources: the Board's 2045 ask ('name and secure its engine before the vote'); rules.md, under which a maker is fitted only if its engine is ready by the airframe's EIS; and company rule 8, under which no engine pushes an airframe's EIS. A failure is a production-readiness soft veto.
tests.numbers:
Current source and default engine:
- The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB only [A-0253]. Company rule 8 makes Rolls-Royce the default engine for an A350 Re-engine.
- Rolls-Royce in 2035: 'Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'.
- Its Trent work (time on wing, life extension, UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet) is fleet support inside the existing budget, 'not a new programme'.

Timing:
- No UltraFan widebody is on the public record.
- Under rules.md an UltraFan WB is ready 6 years after launch. A 2045 launch is ready in 2051, one year after a 2050 EIS.
- To be ready by 2050 it had to launch by 2044, in the 2035 round, and it did not.

Second maker: none on the record.
- The GEnx upgrade (ready 2033) and the Trent 1000 upgrade serve the 787.
- CFM/GE said in 2035: 'no new programmes from us this year'.
- P&W has no widebody engine on this board.

The board prices the Re-engine without an engine, so the grid does not see this gap; production does. A single source would not change the scored enabler, which is narrowbody only.

Ground: readiness, so a soft veto. It does not rest on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch. Margin over the best passing option (hold): +0.89 (S1) / -0.50 (S2), breaking even at 64% S2 and worth +0.40 to +0.54 weighted at 25-35% S2.

Own note: in round 2 I passed a 2035 Re-engine without testing the engine, and the same one-year gap existed then.

tests.name: (8) If the A350 Re-engine is held: compete on A350 and A350F price and product
tests.threshold: No unpriced move draws NGSA or A320neo teams
tests.numbers:
Price and product campaigns run on the A350 commercial and programme teams.
- NGSA development ended in 2036, so nothing is drawn from it.
- The A320neo and NGSA lines are not touched.
- Precedent: the A330neo sold on price against the more efficient 787.
- On the engine side, the product lever available is Rolls-Royce's Trent XWB time-on-wing work inside its own budget.
- The A220-500 stays a study, with no launch this round.

tests.name: (9) NGSA production readiness and engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: NGSA never in service before the technology-ready year (rule 1). On a reported slip, re-time NGSA and never cancel it.
tests.numbers: NGSA has been in service since 2037, inside 'the second half of the 2030s' and after the 2035 technology year, so rule 1 held. No slip is reported, and there is nothing left to re-time.

tests.name: (10) Delay Tactics and cancel (rules 4, 5 and 7; five pillars)
tests.threshold: At most one move, only before fps EIS; poaching only while a programme is in development. Never cancel NGSA.
tests.numbers:
- Delay Tactics: closed. fps has been in service since 2040, only 'none' is open, and none was ordered in any round.
- Cancel: none is listed. Nothing of ours is in development, and rule 7 would bar an NGSA cancel in any case.

tests.name: (11) Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: None is on the record. The lever was 2030-only.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch (development 2045-2049, EIS 2050)

A failed production-readiness test on the engine: no committed engine source ready by EIS 2050.

- No UltraFan widebody is on the public record. Under rules.md one launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, a year after EIS.
- No second maker is on the record.

My capacity (0 years of overlap, $0 strain) and A350F/Spirit absorption tests pass.

This is a soft veto. It does not rest on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch, so it goes through the Board's override review.

Grid margin against the best passing option (hold): +0.89 (S1) / -0.50 (S2), breaking even at 64% S2. That is under the $1B bar in S1, and the item trails hold in the worst plausible column, so no override can carry it. The override budget is unused.

The company's own $1B launch test, which this item also misses by $0.11B, is Toepfer's and Faury's, not mine. Whether to override is Faury's call.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
(a) A committed engine for the A350 Re-engine, ready by its EIS, on the public record before the vote, from Rolls-Royce or a second maker. That turns test 7 into a pass.
- If Rolls-Royce launches an UltraFan widebody in 2045 (ready 2051), a 2050 A350 Re-engine launch (EIS 2055) would pass my engine test.
- It would still have to meet rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record) and the company's $1B test on a fresh grid.
- A second widebody maker committing would make the A350 dual-source, and I would weigh that strongly.

(b) A Rolls-Royce commitment that an upgraded Trent XWB delivers the Re-engine step by 2050. The record is silent on this, and I would need the commitment, not an inference.

(c) A corrected grid showing the Re-engine at least $1B over hold in the expected column, and still ahead of hold in the worst plausible column. My veto is soft, so that would make an override possible. The override is Faury's call.

(d) Toward hold, and harder: a reported supply crunch, a quality event, or a durability problem on the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet. Any of these makes the case against new work non-overridable.

(e) On the hold plan, only a five-pillars flag, and none is on record.

Role-derived tests, Very low confidence: nothing of mine is on record.

Five pillars: no flag on either plan. The brief reports no quality event, safety issue, supply crunch or engine slip. It has no fleet durability data. On the record: NGSA in service since 2037 on CFM plus the Joint Venture engine, and Hot Section kit insertion continuing on the GTF fleet, with no completion figure.

Engines: code locked, two sources, three makers in 2045 and 2050 in both plans. The Joint Venture engine carries 73% of narrowbody engines and inherits GTF2's schedule, so its durability is my first item for the safety review. CFM runs at about a third of its 2026 narrowbody volume. No capacity bind on the record.

Ramp: 1,260 to 1,140 is share times 2,000, not supply.

A350 Re-engine, in service 2050: capacity passes (zero overlap, $0 strain, NGSA teams free since 2036). A350F and Spirit absorption pass. The engine fails. Rolls-Royce, the A350's only source, said in 2035 "no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody" and has launched nothing. On public timing, an UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2051, a year late. No second maker is on record. That is a readiness soft veto, binding; not safety, quality, ramp or crunch. Margin over hold: +0.89 / -0.50; no override reaches $1B. I did not test the engine in 2035. I should have.

Hold passes everything. We compete on A350 price and product with existing teams. The A220-500 stays a study.

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer, and we will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We will take a further step on the A350 only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every lever. The orders are ngsa hold, ngsa_engine_code null (locked at entry into service), rea350 hold and delay_tactics none. There are no Board items and no override.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
(1) Delete red-line and five-pillars breaches. Neither row breaks a pillar.
- Rule 3 holds: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rule 6 holds: one launch, 0 years of overlap.
- Rule 7 holds: no NGSA cancel.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, because fps has been in service since 2040.
- The A350 Re-engine does fail the company's own launch test (profile §6: at least $1B over Do Nothing). It reaches +0.89 at best, short by $0.11B. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].

(2) Survivors: options that pass both colleagues' tests.
- Hold passes every test in both memos.
- The Re-engine carries two binding soft vetoes:
  - Toepfer: the added-move robustness test fails (+0.89 in S1, -0.50 in S2, under $1B in every column);
  - Wagner: engine production readiness fails. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and said 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'. An UltraFan widebody launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051 under rules.md, a year after a 2050 entry into service. No second maker is on the record.
- Neither veto rests on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch.

(3) Highest-grid survivor in the expected column (S1): hold, at +23.37 (S1) and +23.26 (S2). Hold is also the company default, within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.89B). It is the best plan in S2 and the more robust row: its worst column is +23.26, against +22.76.

(4) Override: none is possible.
- The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.89 in S1, under the $1B bar, and -0.50 in S2. Weighted, it is +0.54 / +0.47 / +0.40 at 25 / 30 / 35% S2.
- The Board said it would veto any launch carried by an override.
- The override budget stays unused.

(5) Tie-breaks within $1B all favour hold:
- later capex start: none, against $1.0B a year from 2045;
- strain: equal at $0;
- Board items: 0 against 1 (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn).

WHY, IN MY ORDER
- Five pillars: nothing covert. Safety leads, and the engine-supply report goes to the safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073].
- The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. Joint Venture engine durability and CFM capacity are the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Preparing the Airbus of the next decades: the A350 Re-engine is my derivative instinct [AX-0019, AX-0082]. A derivative without a committed engine is not prepared, and the grid does not clear the company's own bar.
- The Board: it named hold as equally acceptable, and it vetoes nothing in it.

WHAT WE GIVE UP, PLAINLY
- +0.89 in S1, about +0.47 weighted at 30% S2.
- A 2050 return (entry into service 2055) is bounded below about $0.61B on today's mechanics (Toepfer's inference), so in practice we are forgoing the A350 Re-engine for this game.
- I accept that as the doctrine premium. It is within the $1B default; the $3B allowance is not engaged.
- Wagner's own note stands as a lesson: the engine gap existed in 2035 too, so any return now needs a committed engine on the record before the vote.

PACKAGE LINE FOR THE BOARD (no items to vote)
- Five pillars: pass, no flag.
- Toepfer: hold passes all tests. Nil programme cash in 2045-2049 against $5.2B. Worst column S2 at +23.26. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend on the FY2025 floor. Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no buyback proposed.
- Wagner: pass. No quality event, no supply crunch, ramp shield intact. The engine code is locked: 2 sources and 3 makers.
- Grid: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2).
- Re-engine held: +0.89 / -0.50, two soft vetoes respected, no override.
- Rule 3 check: no 787 Re-engine on the record.

Boeing's moves set none of this. The order is the same in both columns.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer (role-derived tests, Low confidence).

On the hold plan everything passes:
- peak cash: $0 against $5.23B;
- plan robustness: worst column S2 at +23.26;
- rule 6, rule 3, the net-cash bridge (net cash every year, payout 30-50%, no equity raise, no dividend cut), the integrity flag, charge presentation and the tie-breaks.

On the A350 Re-engine, five tests pass: peak cash ($1.00B a year, 19% of the line, 0 overlap, $0 strain), plan robustness (+22.76), rule 6, rule 3 and the Board's -$2B downside.

One test fails: added-move robustness, at +0.89 / -0.50. It is under $1B in every column and negative in S2, and it fails the company's launch test by $0.11B.

The soft veto is binding. I accepted it and did not override, because the margin over hold (+0.89 / -0.50, +0.40 to +0.54 weighted) cannot reach $1B and the Board would veto an override. I checked his arithmetic independently: break-even at 64% S2, +0.54 / +0.47 / +0.40. I adopted his bridge, his no-buyback stance and his bound on a 2050 return.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner (role-derived tests, Very low confidence; the record holds nothing of his own).

These pass on both plans: five pillars and quality (no flag, no event on the record), engine supply on NGSA (2 sources and 3 makers, code locked), the ramp shield (the fall from 1,260 to 1,140 is share times 2,000, not supply), engineering capacity and rule 6 (0 overlap, NGSA teams free since 2036), A350F and Spirit absorption, and price-and-product competition if the Re-engine is held. No supply crunch is reported.

One test fails on the Re-engine: engine production readiness. There is no committed engine source ready by a 2050 entry into service. Rolls-Royce is the only A350 source and plans no new widebody programme. An UltraFan widebody launched in 2045 is ready in 2051 (I checked this against rules.md). No second maker is on the record.

It is a readiness soft veto, binding, and not a safety, quality, ramp or crunch ground. I accepted it. No override can carry the item (+0.89 under $1B, -0.50 in S2), and the Board said it would veto one.

I adopted his safety-review report and his candour that the same gap existed in 2035. A committed engine is now a condition of any Re-engine return.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold), at about 70%. Boeing's stated priority is 737 MAX and 787 production stability and growing the current 787 out of Charleston. The GEnx upgrade has served the 787 since 2033, and Rolls-Royce plans no new widebody programme.

S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) is about 30% (range 25-35%). It is more plausible than in 2035 because Boeing's fps cash peak (2036-37) is past, and it is the worst plausible column for both plans.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
The best plan in S1 is NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine, at +24.26 (S1) and +22.76 (S2). It is not a survivor: it carries two binding soft vetoes (Toepfer's added-move robustness test and Wagner's engine readiness test), it fails the company's $1B launch test by $0.11B, and no override can carry it.

The chosen plan is the highest-grid survivor and the company default: NGSA hold + A350 hold, at +23.37 (S1) and +23.26 (S2). It is also the best plan in S2.
decision.objective_note:
These objectives are scored by the GM; they never change the payoff.
- Defend 60/40: not met. Narrowbody share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050, and no option this round reaches it, because the only open lever is widebody.
- Protect the A320 family: met at 60% before NGSA's entry into service.
- Enabler (stable engine supply): met in both plans and both columns. NGSA has 2 sources (CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and 3 narrowbody makers (CFM, P&W, RR) are in the market in 2045 and 2050.
- The NGSA engine code is locked, so our orders this round can trigger no conditional engine launch.
- No PV, cash or integrity was traded for any objective.
decision.predictions:
Boeing:
- About 70%: Boeing holds the 787 and keeps growing its rate out of Charleston, with no Rate Increase.
- About 30%: it launches a 787 Re-engine with entry into service in 2050. That costs our hold plan only $0.11B (to +23.26) and closes any A350 Re-engine return under rule 3.

Our position:

final.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer, and we will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We will take a further step on the A350 only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
final.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every lever. The orders are ngsa hold, ngsa_engine_code null (locked at entry into service), rea350 hold and delay_tactics none. There are no Board items and no override.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
(1) Delete red-line and five-pillars breaches. Neither row breaks a pillar.
- Rule 3 holds: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rule 6 holds: one launch, 0 years of overlap.
- Rule 7 holds: no NGSA cancel.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, because fps has been in service since 2040.
- The A350 Re-engine does fail the company's own launch test (profile §6: at least $1B over Do Nothing). It reaches +0.89 at best, short by $0.11B. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].

(2) Survivors: options that pass both colleagues' tests.
- Hold passes every test in both memos.
- The Re-engine carries two binding soft vetoes:
  - Toepfer: the added-move robustness test fails (+0.89 in S1, -0.50 in S2, under $1B in every column);
  - Wagner: engine production readiness fails. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and said 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'. An UltraFan widebody launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051 under rules.md, a year after a 2050 entry into service. No second maker is on the record.
- Neither veto rests on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch.

(3) Highest-grid survivor in the expected column (S1): hold, at +23.37 (S1) and +23.26 (S2). Hold is also the company default, within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.89B). It is the best plan in S2 and the more robust row: its worst column is +23.26, against +22.76.

(4) Override: none is possible.
- The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.89 in S1, under the $1B bar, and -0.50 in S2. Weighted, it is +0.54 / +0.47 / +0.40 at 25 / 30 / 35% S2.
- The Board said it would veto any launch carried by an override.
- The override budget stays unused.

(5) Tie-breaks within $1B all favour hold:
- later capex start: none, against $1.0B a year from 2045;
- strain: equal at $0;
- Board items: 0 against 1 (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn).

WHY, IN MY ORDER
- Five pillars: nothing covert. Safety leads, and the engine-supply report goes to the safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073].
- The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. Joint Venture engine durability and CFM capacity are the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Preparing the Airbus of the next decades: the A350 Re-engine is my derivative instinct [AX-0019, AX-0082]. A derivative without a committed engine is not prepared, and the grid does not clear the company's own bar.
- The Board: it named hold as equally acceptable, and it vetoes nothing in it.

WHAT WE GIVE UP, PLAINLY
- +0.89 in S1, about +0.47 weighted at 30% S2.
- A 2050 return (entry into service 2055) is bounded below about $0.61B on today's mechanics (Toepfer's inference), so in practice we are forgoing the A350 Re-engine for this game.
- I accept that as the doctrine premium. It is within the $1B default; the $3B allowance is not engaged.
- Wagner's own note stands as a lesson: the engine gap existed in 2035 too, so any return now needs a committed engine on the record before the vote.

PACKAGE LINE FOR THE BOARD (no items to vote)
- Five pillars: pass, no flag.
- Toepfer: hold passes all tests. Nil programme cash in 2045-2049 against $5.2B. Worst column S2 at +23.26. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend on the FY2025 floor. Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no buyback proposed.
- Wagner: pass. No quality event, no supply crunch, ramp shield intact. The engine code is locked: 2 sources and 3 makers.
- Grid: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2).
- Re-engine held: +0.89 / -0.50, two soft vetoes respected, no override.
- Rule 3 check: no 787 Re-engine on the record.

Boeing's moves set none of this. The order is the same in both columns.

Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`lobby_emissions: launch`. On its own it costs $1B and does nothing on the board, so it fails 'paid for the risk' and our rule that Lobby goes only with an Open Fan launched this round or live. Its +4.38 beside the Open Fan only softens a penalty the Open Fan itself creates, and the pair is -21.89 on an $11B bill. If the Open Fan is vetoed, we veto Lobby with it at review. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

Any `cancel`, should one be put forward. None is on the menu: all three programmes are ready. A cancel of an engine that live airframes fly would also fail hard rule 5, our cancellation test and the CFM parity rule.

recommendations.text:
Safety and quality, in service.
- The Ducted flies on both new narrowbodies, and Embraer counts beside it. Bring Ali's fleet durability report to the full board: time on wing, shop visits, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, not analysis.
- Make every finding a cross-functional call, and fix the part rather than redesign or cancel.
- Bring us at once any durability finding that touches both aircraft. Fleet support comes before any new spend.

Delivery, framed for the customer. Both aircraft are now shared three ways, and the Joint Venture has formed. Keep CFM's place through readiness, durability and support, not through price: we are not going for share, and there is no birthright.
- Re-base the joint capacity plan with Safran on the grid's volume: 1,079 CFM narrowbody engines a year from 2040, against 3,040 to 2036.
- Original equipment comes before spares, and capex stays within 2-3% of revenue.
- No capacity or rate number goes out until each airframer's volumes are agreed.

RISE.
- Keep it funded as technology inside the R&D we protect first: no cancel for cost and no 'program dividend'.
- In the `objective_note`, say plainly that 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' can no longer be met: a 2045 launch is ready in 2055.
- Say also that a 2050 launch would still wait. On our arithmetic it would be about -17B against hold, over its $8B bill (inference). Do not stretch the test in the last round either.
- Report Ali's gates (flight test, compact-core turn-off, more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test) as the state of the technology. Keep the RISE allowance unspent.

Cost and capital.
- A hold commits no new R&D. Keep the 70% payout and the A-range rating whole, and do not redeploy the room into a product the grid shows waiting.
- State the premium in dollars: $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. Show the RISE allowance separately at $0 of $15B.
- Book at or below -69.69. Carry the off-grid widebody exposure (about $0.8-1.1B, inference) as the labelled low case.
- Last round's -77 booking proved on the right side when the Joint Venture formed.

Objective, NB share of at least 50%. Say plainly that the share is 27.0% from 2040 and that no lever on this round's menu moves it. Spend no premium on it. Commercial work on both aircraft stays on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept out of the public statement.

CFM parity rule (Safran consent).
- On a hold, record in the rationale that fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice.
- Safran cannot be consulted in this game, so assert no Safran position.
- Any Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path. We know of none on the record.

Public statement.
- Name no rival, the Joint Venture included, and blame no one.
- Give no Open Fan entry year: 'our customers decide when' is enough.
- No CFM price, rate or capacity number without Safran.
- Claim the Ducted's in-service record only as far as field and test evidence has earned it, and never call it next-generation.
- Replace last round's 'last year of development' line.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

On this board the narrowbody game is settled. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service: NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040. Each is fitted with all three makers, and neither code can change after entry into service. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and its engine has been ready since 2036. No order left on our menu buys back a point of NB share.

So the game is the installed base we have, not the share we don't. That means:
- 1,079 CFM narrowbody engines a year, on two aircraft we share three ways;
- the LEAP fleet behind them;
- 152 widebody engines a year, with the GEnx upgrade counting since 2042.
"Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422]. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages." [CX-0630]

We win it on execution, in this order: safety, quality, delivery and cost [CX-0658].
- The Ducted earns its durability record in service on both aircraft, on field data, not analysis [CX-0009].
- OE delivery comes before spares, and support earns the next order. We have no birthright [CX-0564, CX-0529].
- RISE stays whole as technology for the airframe that comes after these two [CX-0214, CX-0469].

The question for this room has two parts.
1. Does anything on this grid pay us to move? I don't think so, and I want you to try to break that.
2. If not, where does the work go? I'd say fleet durability, and a capacity plan re-based to the volume we actually have. And we say plainly that both objective legs are out of reach by any order.
levers_in_play: ducted: hold only. Ready since 2036 and in service on both new aircraft, with its +10 pp NB counting. It can no longer be cancelled.

open_fan: hold | launch. $8B, ready at launch + 10, so 2055. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are already in service, so the 35 pp wait penalty applies (20 pp with Lobby), and it takes our 27% NB share to zero for the rest of the window. The only route around H2 is the one RISE allowance, up to $15B.
partner_embraer: hold only. Counting since 2037, +5 pp NB. It can no longer be cancelled.
lobby_emissions: hold | launch. $1B, plus the $2B strain on the Board's reading (Ghai to confirm). It only caps the Open Fan loss: worth +4.38 inside the Open Fan row, and nothing on its own.
genx: hold only. The upgrade has counted since 2042, +5 pp WB. GE alone, so no Safran gate.
cancel: not offered. All three programmes are ready. H5 stands on RISE regardless.
options_to_test:
Row A: hold everything, the reference row (Do Nothing).
- S1: -69.69 (56.4%). It is the best plan in the only column, so it is 0.00 against Do Nothing in both the expected and the worst column, and the premium is $0.
- It keeps the Ducted, Embraer and GEnx counting.
- No new R&D is committed, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched.

Row B: Open Fan.
- S1: -95.96 (40.0%), which is -26.27 against hold.
- The bill is $8B. The other $18.27B is the wait penalty: CFM's 27% NB share goes to zero for 2045-2056. My check gives $18.28B, on 1,079 engines a year for 12 years.
- It would be ready in 2055: 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's. H2 binds.
- The only route is the RISE allowance, and that would need $26.27B against a $15B cap.
- It also can't meet the objective, since 2055 is after 2050. It fails every test I hold.

Row C: Open Fan + Lobby, the cheapest Open Fan row.
- S1: -91.58 (42.8%), which is -21.89 against hold. Lobby is worth +4.38 inside the row.
- On the Board's reading the bill is $11B ($8B + $1B + $2B strain), so it loses $10.89B beyond its bill.
- It would need $21.89B of RISE allowance, $6.89B over the cap.
- I test it only to put a dollar figure on the Open Fan leg of the objective, and it can't meet that leg either.
Excluded: Lobby alone. It is not on the grid. It costs $1B (or $3B if the strain applies) and does nothing on the board. Doctrine allows Lobby only with an Open Fan launched or live.

Forward look, not a row: an Open Fan launched in the 2050 round would be ready in 2060 and would still wait. On my arithmetic it is about -17B against hold: $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56 plus the $8B bill (inference; it matches the Board's figure). So RISE stays technology to the end of this game, and we don't stretch the test in the last round either.

Other moves to test (the board does not price them; Ghai and Ali to check):
(1) Ali's fleet durability report to the full Board on the Ducted (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040) and the Embraer application. It covers time on wing, shop visits, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence. Every finding is a cross-functional call [CX-0012], and we fix the part [CX-0005].
(2) The joint CFM capacity plan, re-based with Safran on the grid's volume: 1,079 NB engines a year from 2040, against 3,040 to 2036. OE comes before spares [CX-0529], we go lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653], and no number goes out in public.
(3) Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP and GEnx fleets, on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept private [CX-0184, CX-0609]. This is the installed-base work the game now turns on [CX-0422].
(4) RISE kept funded as technology, with the gates reported as the state of the technology and no product date. Its technology keeps flowing into upgrades for the in-service fleet where test supports it [CX-0162].
(5) The CFM parity record for a hold.
red_lines: Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No programme is carried on in service, and nothing is launched, while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands without a cross-functional answer on evidence [CX-0012]. Ramp and schedule never trade against safety [CX-0603].
My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn or for schedule [CX-0208]. In service, that means we fix the part, not redesign or cancel the engine [CX-0005].

My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation. The Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0183] and stands only as an H3 defence, so we never call it next-generation.
H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. CFM support stands on both aircraft and on Embraer.

H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. Both new narrowbodies are in service long before a 2055 Open Fan, so there is no launch. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance (up to $15B), and the cheapest row needs $21.89B.
H3: a Ducted only as a defence. The trigger was met and the engine is in service. We make no new Ducted claim beyond that.
H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it, and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398].
H6, through Ali's test: no date or durability claim without test or field evidence [CX-0009]. No Open Fan entry year, and no time-on-wing claim for the Ducted that the field data hasn't earned.

H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. An Open Fan launch with no airframer path needs a stated reason why Safran would agree, and we have none. Rate, capacity and price commitments are made only jointly. GEnx is GE alone.
H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals, the Joint Venture included [CX-0625, CX-0580].

H9: the doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. Running count: $0 of $2.0B and $0 of $4.0B. The one RISE allowance (up to $15B) is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and it is unspent.
frame.asks_cfo:
Rahul, on its face this is a hold round. Tell me where that breaks, in dollars.

(1) Each row against hold in S1. S1 is the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column.
- Open Fan is -26.27. Confirm my split: the $8B bill plus an $18.27B wait penalty (27% NB to zero for 2045-2056; my check gives $18.28B).
- Open Fan + Lobby is -21.89. Confirm whether Lobby triggers the $2B strain. The Board reads an $11B bill and $10.89B beyond it, and Lobby is worth +4.38 inside the row.
- Lobby alone is not on the grid. Price it at $1B, or $3B with strain, for nothing on the board.

(2) Premium. Hold is the best plan, so the premium is $0. Confirm the counts:
- $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game;
- the RISE allowance at $0 of $15B. The cheapest Open Fan row needs $21.89B, which is over it.

(3) Booking. Plan on the low case [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Last round we said we would raise to S1 once the codes locked [CX-0654], and they have. The NB side is now locked. The remaining exposure is off-grid widebody, on my arithmetic (inference):
- a Trent 1000 upgrade, about $0.80B PV, counting from 2048;
- an UltraFan WB after a Re-engine, about $1.13B, counting from 2051.
Both rival makers' statements and both airframers' statements argue against these. I lean to booking -71, which is hold less the larger exposure, rounded down. Challenge it, and size anything else off-grid you see, such as a lone Re-engine moving airframe share on the 787.

(4) Your binding tests on a hold:
- pays for itself, with no new R&D;
- volumes first;

- the 70% payout and the A-range rating whole [CX-0645].

(5) Capacity. BOARD GUIDANCE asks us to re-base the joint plan with Safran on 1,079 CFM NB engines a year from 2040, against 3,040 to 2036.
- Is that inside your rule of no number until each airframer's volumes are agreed [CX-0944]?
- Does capex stay within 2-3% of revenue?

(6) Terms. Does fleet support and aftermarket on both aircraft, on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept private [CX-0184, CX-0609], pass your price/cost test?

(7) The objective in dollars:
- No order can buy the Open Fan leg.
- The NB leg is 23 pp short, and no lever moves it.
- The objective premium is $0.
Also check my forward look: a 2050 Open Fan would be about -$17B against hold (inference). That way we don't revisit it in the last round on hope.

(8) BOARD GUIDANCE (labelled, non-binding): it would veto any `open_fan` or `lobby_emissions` launch, any item with a premium and any cancel. Tell me if any of your tests disagrees with that. If you hold a binding veto on anything, give it to me with the numbers.
frame.asks_ops:
Mohamed, I need to feel it, see it, smell it [CX-0259]. Give me test and field data, not analysis [CX-0009].

(1) Fleet durability. The Ducted has been in service on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. BOARD GUIDANCE asks for your report to the full Board on time on wing, shop visits, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings.

- If the brief carries no field data, say so plainly. Then tell me what you would measure and against what yardstick, for example field cycles against the CFM56, as with LEAP [CX-0006].
- Do the same for the Embraer application.

(2) Flags. Do you raise any safety or durability flag on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx? If so, give me the cross-functional answer [CX-0012].

- 'No flag' is not a clearance, and I won't read it as one.

(3) GEnx has counted since 2042. Do you see any date issue, or any Re-engine on the record that would change it? I see none.

(4) Open Fan. Confirm that:

BOARD GUIDANCE (labelled): it would veto any Open Fan launch, alone or with Lobby.

(5) RISE gates: flight test; compact-core durability turned on and turned off; more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test; noise below today's LEAP. Report what the record shows now, as the state of the technology and not as a product case. Where the record is silent, say so. Promise no RISE date.

(6) Supply load. A hold adds no project. The load now is fleet support:
