OE comes before spares [CX-0529]. Give me the data to re-base the joint capacity plan at 1,079 NB engines a year, with no number in public. I'll check it against doctrine and take a quarter to a half off any ramp promise [CX-0590, CX-0592].

(7) Public line. Last round's 'in its last year of development' has to go. Does this pass your test: 'Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says'? Name any time-on-wing or durability wording you would veto. Does 'RISE remains our next generation; our customers decide when' still pass?
frame.initial_lean:
This is a lean, not a decision; your memos decide it. I lean to HOLD EVERYTHING: all five fields at `hold`.

DUCTED, EMBRAER, GEnx: HOLD. That is the only option for each. All three are ready and counting.

OPEN FAN: HOLD.
- H2 binds in the only column. Both new narrowbodies are in service, and a 2045 launch is ready in 2055.
- My installed-base lens pulls at me again: OE losses as "seeding the next 20, the next 30 years" [CX-0555]. But the board counts NB only to 2056, and the cheapest row is $6.89B over the RISE allowance. The cap holds.
- RISE stays funded as technology: no cancel (H5) and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214].

LOBBY: HOLD. It does nothing without a live Open Fan.

EXPECTED COLUMN AND BOOKING (preliminary)
- Expected column S1, weight 1.00, since it is the only column the GM gave. Off-grid moves are named and labelled, never weighted into it.
- I book about -71: hold less the larger off-grid widebody exposure, rounded down. That raises last round's -77 now that the codes have locked [CX-0654].
- Premium $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance is $0 of $15B, unspent.

OBJECTIVE. I say it plainly:
- NB share is 27.0% from 2040 against the 50% target, and no lever on this menu moves it.
- 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' can't be met by any order.
- No objective premium is spent.

SAFRAN GATE. There is no new CFM narrowbody order. Fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice: both airframers fly CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219]. I assert no Safran position. GEnx is GE alone.

OTHER MOVES
- Ali's fleet durability report to the full Board.
- A joint capacity plan re-based to 1,079 NB engines a year, with no new facility and no public number.
- Fleet support on standard terms, priced jointly.
- RISE gates reported as the state of the technology.

PUBLIC LINE
- Safety first, and what we know and what we don't [CX-0436].
- The Ducted is in service on both aircraft, and its record gets earned in the field.
- We keep our place on readiness, durability and support, with no birthright.
- RISE remains our next generation, and our customers decide when.
- No rival named, no blame, no price or rate without our partner.
It's that simple, ain't that hard.

tests.name: Pays for itself (price/cost positive in PV form; binding: capex)
tests.threshold: Each launch must beat hold in the expected column with its bill charged in full: Open Fan $8B, Lobby $1B, plus $2B of strain where the grid charges it. S1 is the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column. Binding: capex (inference: the PV form of my price/cost rule).
tests.numbers:
Hold everything passes: it is the best row at -69.69 (56.4%), 0.00 against Do Nothing, with no new R&D. Both alternatives fail.

Ask (1), each row against hold in S1:
- Open Fan: -95.96, so -26.27. Your split is confirmed: the $8B bill plus an $18.27B wait penalty. My check is $18.28B: 1,079 NB engines a year at $3.74M x 1.6, inflated 2.2% a year and discounted at 8.5% to 2026, lost for 2045-2056. That puts the row at -26.28 against the grid's -26.27.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -91.58, so -21.89. I correct the bill: it is $9B ($8B + $1B), not $11B. The grid charges the $2B strain once, and it already sits in hold (strain -2.00). With Lobby, CFM keeps 7.9% of NB (8.33 of 105 pp before renormalisation) rather than 0%. That is a loss of $12.90B of NB value, so the row is -9.00 - 12.90 = -21.90 against the grid's -21.89. With a second $2B strain it would be -23.90, which the grid does not show. The pair therefore loses $12.89B beyond its $9B bill, not $10.89B beyond $11B (inference: reconciliation of the grid).
- Lobby inside the row: +4.38, which is $5.38B of NB value saved less the $1B.
- Lobby alone is not on the grid. It costs $1B with no board effect and no second strain, so it is -1.00 (inference). It is not $3B.
No row beats hold, so the only possible Board items fail.

tests.name: Volumes first (binding: capex)
tests.threshold: Judge a move in the columns consistent with the public record. A launch that beats hold only by assuming a selection not on the record fails. For a capacity or rate plan, no number before each airframer's volumes are agreed. Binding: capex (inference).
tests.numbers:
Hold launches nothing.

The record: NGSA has been in service since 2037 and fps since 2040, both on code 7 (CFM + P&W + RR). Both codes are now locked. S1 is the record.

The Open Fan has no airframer path. No new narrowbody enters service after 2040, and a 2045 launch is ready in 2055. It beats hold in no column, so no selection could rescue it.

Ask (5), capacity:
- The 1,079 is the board's volume (27.0% x 4,000 NB engines). It is not an airframer's agreed schedule. Boeing lets stable production and its KPIs set rates; Airbus plans a disciplined, controlled ramp. Neither has given us a rate.
- A private planning basis on 1,079, built jointly with Safran, is inside my rule. A number to an airframer or in public before each airframer's volumes are worked is not.
- The plan re-bases down: 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year we delivered to 2036. So the risk is stranded capacity, not a missed ramp.

tests.name: No overcapitalization (capex analogy for R&D; binding under the GM's team rule, advice under this round's decision rule)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over the development years, stays within about $2.5B a year. That is the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 FCF. Facilities capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, with no overcapitalization. It cannot fail on the board's numbers.
tests.numbers:
Ask (4):
- Hold commits $0 of new R&D. The development stack is finished: the Ducted was ready in 2036, Embraer has counted since 2037, and GEnx was ready in 2033. The 70% payout and the A-range rating are whole.
- For reference, the Open Fan would be $0.8B a year ($8B over 10 years). With Lobby it is $0.9B a year on the grid's $9B bill, or $1.8B in 2045 if Lobby's $1B lands at once. The Board's reading is $1.1B a year. All of these are under $2.5B, so this test does not rescue either item.

Ask (5), capex and facilities:
- The board has no revenue or capex line. Its engine lifecycle value falls from 25.8 nominal $B (2036) to 13.9 (2045), against 31.3 in the status quo. A footprint built for 3,040 NB engines a year is about 2.8 times what the grid needs.
- No new facility: lean before capital. Capex stays inside 2-3% of revenue and goes to MRO turnaround on the fleet we have, not to OE lines.
- The installed base delivered 2026-2044 is about 45,000 CFM NB engines on the brief's counts (33,440 to 2036, 6,133 in 2037-39 and 5,395 in 2040-44).

Analyst context, not the board: GE returned about 94-124% of FCF in the MS model, so any unbudgeted spend comes out of buybacks.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (advice)
tests.threshold: Name the recommended plan's worst column, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores. Advice, not binding.
tests.numbers:
Hold's worst column is S1 at -69.69. It is also the expected column, so the gap is 0.00. Everything below is off-grid and labelled; none of it is weighted into a column.

Ask (3), off-grid widebody exposure (inference, on the published share rules):
- UltraFan WB after a Re-engine (counting from 2051): $1.08B on renormalised shares (CFM from 44.8% to 35.2% of WB), or $1.13B on your flat 10 pp.
- Trent 1000 upgrade (counting from 2048): $0.76B renormalised (44.8% to 40.0%), or $0.80B on your flat 5 pp.
- The rules make these two exclusive, so they do not stack. The maximum is about $1.1B.
- If either is ordered in the 2050 round instead: T1000 counting from 2053 is $0.41B; UltraFan WB after a 2050 Re-engine, counting from 2056, is $0.50B.
- A lone Re-engine: the published rules map no WB airframe share to engine share, and CFM's WB share stayed at 42.0% while the airframe split was flat. So I cannot size it. The sensitivity is about $0.13B per point of WB engine share over 2050-2061. It is unsized and not booked.

The board also leaves out:
- An airframer delivery slowdown, tariffs or a recession. The board holds NB at 2,000 aircraft a year. A 10% delivery shortfall would cost about $1.8B of NB value (2045-56) and $1.0B of WB value (2045-61).
- A fleet durability finding on the Ducted across both aircraft. There is no board lever for it, and its cost is not on the grid. If one is found, we book the reserve in the quarter we find the need. Each point of NB share over 2045-56 is worth about $0.68B.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence (advice)
tests.threshold: For each programme: bill year, ready year and first year of share gain, all inside the horizon (NB to 2056, WB to 2061). Advice.
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: billed in 2030 ($4B) and ready in 2036, with NB share gains since 2037. It is paying.
- Embraer: counting since 2037 (+5 pp NB), with no R&D on the board.
- GEnx upgrade: ready in 2033 and counting since 2042, taking WB share from 42.0% to 44.8% through 2061.
- Open Fan launched in 2045: billed in 2045 ($8B) and ready in 2055. It gains no share on the board and loses from 2045, so it has no profitable year inside the NB window.

Forward look (ask 7, inference):
- A 2050 Open Fan is $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56 plus the $8B bill, so -17.05 against hold. Your figure is confirmed.
- A 2050 Open Fan + Lobby is $6.39B plus $9B, so -15.39. That is over the $15B allowance, and it would be ready in 2060, after the NB window closes in 2056.
- Neither can meet 'ready by 2050'.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan that stacks two or more projects (the $2B strain). GE9X losses are not treated as live. Advice.
tests.numbers:
Hold adds no project. The one $2B strain was charged for the 2030 stack (Ducted, Embraer, GEnx) and sits in hold at -2.00.

Ask (1), the strain: an Open Fan + Lobby would stack two projects in 2045. The grid's reconciliation shows that the board charges no second $2B (inference). In real life, though, the load sits on top of the Ducted's first shop visits on two aircraft, the LEAP aftermarket, GE9X and the durability kits. That supply load is Ali's ground.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (binding: capex)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium of at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan. Binding: capex (inference).
tests.numbers:
Ask (2): hold is the best plan, so the premium is $0.00. The counts are confirmed: $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance is $0 of $15B, unspent.

The cheapest Open Fan row needs $21.89B, which is $6.89B over the allowance and $19.89B over the general cap.

Ask (7), the objective in dollars:
- Open Fan leg: no order can buy it. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055.
- NB 50% leg: 27.0% from 2040 is 23 pp short. For scale only, 23 pp over 2045-56 would be worth about $15.6B (at $0.68B a point), but no lever on this menu moves a point.
- Objective premium: $0.

tests.name: Terms (Safran gate on price; binding: terms)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession and no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran, in any public statement or other move. Binding: terms (inference).
tests.numbers:
This is provisional; I re-run it on the exact statement and other moves at the veto check.

Ask (6): fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP and GEnx fleets, on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept private, passes. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision, and the partners split CFM-performed LEAP shop visits equally. The conditions:
- no price used to buy back NB share. Share pricing would be a concession, and profitability is more important than share;
- durability fixes go through reserves and existing service agreements as contracted, not as a commercial giveaway;
- service contracts are modelled conservatively.

Your planned public line carries no price, rate or capacity number and names no rival, so it passes.

Safran-gate line for a hold: fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice. No Safran position is asserted. GEnx is GE alone.

tests.name: Guide low (advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV, at the low end of the expected column, with no upside booked before it is confirmed. Advice.
tests.numbers:
Ask (3): book -71.
- That is hold at -69.69 less the larger off-grid WB exposure ($1.13B on your arithmetic, $1.08B on mine), which gives -70.82, rounded down to -71.
- The two WB exposures are exclusive under the rules, so they don't stack. -71 covers the larger one with $0.18-0.23B to spare.
- The raise from -77 is earned. Last round I said we would raise once the codes locked, and they have. The -77 booking covered the Joint Venture with $7.31B to spare.
- Don't book above -69.69. The unsized items (a lone Re-engine, a delivery slowdown) are named as the low case, not booked.

tests.name: Board guidance cross-check (ask 8; advice)
tests.threshold: Does any of my tests disagree with the Board's guidance (labelled, non-binding)? Advice.
tests.numbers:
There is no disagreement on any verdict. My binding tests veto the same items: any open_fan launch, any lobby_emissions launch, and any item carrying a premium.

One correction for the record, which does not change the verdict. The grid shows no second $2B strain for Lobby. The Open Fan + Lobby bill is $9B, and the row loses $12.89B beyond it, not $10.89B beyond $11B. The payout-floor figure becomes $0.9B a year (or $1.8B in 2045), still under $2.5B.

Mix (ask 5): fewer OE engines mean fewer OE losses near term. But the board books each engine's aftermarket at delivery (the 1.6 multiplier). So the shop visits on the fleet we've delivered are already inside the -69.69: the work protects that value, it doesn't add to it. NB PV over 2045-56 is $18.28B on hold, against $51.5B at the status-quo 3,040 a year.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch. Culp's lean holds it, so this veto is not triggered.
vetoes.ground:
Capex. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.
- It fails pays-for-itself: Open Fan is -26.27 against hold in S1, the only column ($8B bill plus an $18.27B wait penalty). Open Fan + Lobby is -21.89 ($9B bill plus a $12.89B loss; the grid charges no second strain).
- It fails volumes-first: no airframer path. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are in service long before a 2055 ready year.
- Its premium is at least $21.89B against the best non-RISE plan. That is over the $2.0B cap and $6.89B over the $15B RISE allowance (hard rule 9).

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch, with or without the Open Fan.
vetoes.ground:
Capex. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.
- On its own it costs $1B with no board effect: -1.00 in S1 (inference; it is not a grid row).
- Inside the Open Fan row it is worth +4.38, but only against a penalty the Open Fan creates, and it falls with the Open Fan.
- It beats hold in no column.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing, a price concession or price used to buy back NB share, or that talks CFM narrowbody price, rate or capacity without Safran.
vetoes.ground: Terms. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran, and launch-era pricing is behind us. This is provisional: I re-run it on the exact statement and other moves at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: A capacity or rate number, given to an airframer or in public, before that airframer's volumes are worked, or any new facility in the re-based plan.
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto: it falls outside my binding grounds unless it carries price. No number goes out before the airframer's volumes are agreed. The grid's volume is 1,079 CFM NB engines a year, 35.5% of the 3,040 we built for, so new capacity would overcapitalise.

vetoes.plan: expected_pv_b booked above -69.69, or above -71 without a stated reason.
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. Guide low: book -71, which is hold less the larger, exclusive off-grid WB exposure (about $1.1B). Label a lone Re-engine (about $0.13B per WB point) and a delivery slowdown as the low case.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- **Hold.** Nothing on this grid would. If Ali raises a fleet durability finding on the Ducted across both aircraft, I would book the reserve in the quarter we find the need and keep fleet support ahead of any new spend. It is his ground, and it would not change the orders.
- **Open Fan.** It would take an airframer on the record wanting a new narrowbody that enters service after the Open Fan is ready, and a grid row within $15B of the best non-RISE plan. Neither is in sight. The 2050 rows I compute are -17.05 (Open Fan) and -15.39 (with Lobby), both over the allowance and ready after the NB window.
- **Booking.** A Re-engine or a Trent 1000 upgrade on the record would make me book that exposure in full: about $1.1B or $0.8B, which takes the booking toward -71 or below. An airframer delivery cut would make me book the volume loss, about $0.18B NB per 1% over 2045-56.
- **Capacity.** Once each airframer's rates are agreed, I would put a joint number on the plan with Safran, and not before.
- **Lobby strain.** If the GM confirms that Lobby triggers a second $2B strain, the Open Fan + Lobby bill becomes $11B. The verdict stays the same.
cfo.memo:
Larry, I tried to break it, and it holds. There's nothing to hide in the numbers.

One column, and hold is the best row at -69.69. Open Fan is -26.27: the $8B bill plus $18.27B of wait penalty, our 1,079 engines a year going to zero for 2045-56. I get $18.28B. Open Fan + Lobby is -21.89, but the bill is $9B, not $11B. The grid charges strain once, and that $2B already sits in hold. The row reconciles to a cent with no second strain, so the pair loses $12.89B beyond its bill, not $10.89B. The verdict doesn't change, and it is $6.89B over the RISE allowance. Lobby alone is $1B for nothing.

Premium: $0 of $2.0B, $0 of $4.0B, RISE $0 of $15B. No new R&D, so the 70% payout and the rating are whole.

A 2050 Open Fan: -17.05, as you have it. With Lobby it's -15.39, still over the allowance, and ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes. We're not expecting that this magically gets better.

Booking: -71 is right. The two widebody exposures are exclusive under the rules, so they don't stack, and the larger is about $1.1B.

Capacity: plan privately with Safran on 1,079, no new facility, no number out. The good news is the shop visits on the fleet we've already delivered. But the board counts them at delivery, so this work protects the -69.69; it doesn't add to it.

Hold everything.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my veto: dates)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts 7 years after launch; GEnx 3 years after launch, counting from the first Re-engine's entry or 2042. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (2030 + 6). Partner Embraer: launched 2030, counts 2037 (2030 + 7), after the 2036 engine it rides on. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033 (2030 + 3); it counts from 2042 because there is no Re-engine on the record (WB 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042 in the brief). Open Fan, held. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 (2045 + 10, which clears the 2045 floor). A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. Rows A (-69.69), B (-95.96) and C (-91.58) all use these years, and no row's value rests on an earlier year. The date ground passes for every row; Row B and Row C fail on the airframe test below, not on the date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my veto: dates), with the public-line check (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: Every date or durability claim in the public statement or other moves must be one a test or field data backs: no Open Fan entry year, no ready date before launch plus development years, no time-on-wing, cycle, shop-visit or durability claim for the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx that field data has not earned, no RISE flight-test year, no fuel-burn number given as a result, and no capacity or ramp date.
tests.numbers: Culp's draft: (a) 'Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft.' That is the public record, not a test claim: CFM's new engine was ready in 2036, before NGSA's entry (2037) and fps's (2040), and the bulletin shows CFM fitted on both. Pass. (b) 'Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says.' A commitment with no number. It is my habit of reporting back against the promise [CX-0007]. Pass. (c) 'RISE remains our next generation; our customers decide when.' No date, and next-generation is held for the open fan on physics. Pass. (d) Replacing 'in its last year of development' is right: the engine is ready, so the line is out of date. Wording I would veto at step 4 on binding ground 2: any cycle count or time-on-wing figure; 'mature time on wing'; 'proven durability'; 'matching' or 'beating' the CFM56; any shop-visit interval or 'x times better'; a date for a durability kit; a RISE flight-test year; an Open Fan entry or ready year (2055 included); '20% better fuel burn' stated as a result; any capacity or rate number or ramp date. Also, no claim that the Ducted holds or wins NB share (see the reconciliation in the Ducted airframe test).

tests.name: Fleet durability report: Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application, GEnx (Culp's asks 1 and 2; the Board's item 4)
tests.threshold: Report on field data and turn-on, turn-off evidence, never analysis. Where the brief carries no field data, say so plainly and name what will be measured and against what yardstick.
tests.numbers: What the record shows: no field data. The brief and bulletin carry no time on wing, no shop visits, no life-limited parts at full life and no inspection findings for the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx. Years in service by 2045: Ducted on NGSA 8 (since 2037) and on fps 5 (since 2040); Embraer counting 8 (since 2037); GEnx upgrade ready 12 (2033), counting 3 (2042). What I bring the full Board: (1) time on wing: fleet-leader and fleet-average cycles to first shop visit, by airframe (NGSA, fps, Embraer) and by environment, with hot and harsh (Middle East, India) kept separate [CX-0161]; (2) the yardstick: the CFM56 in the same environment, as with LEAP: 9,882 cycles against about 17,000, and about 4,800-5,000 against 7,000-8,000 in hot and harsh [CX-0006]; the LEAP-1A kit's twofold gain to CFM56 parity [CX-0209] is the floor a new engine should not fall below (inference); (3) shop visits: unscheduled removal rate and removal causes by part number, looking for the small handful of parts [CX-0161]; (4) life-limited parts at full life: inspection findings against certified life; (5) enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO [CX-0010]; (6) every field distress turned on in test and turned off by the fix before I believe it [CX-0009], with root cause and the fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator [CX-0003]. Embraer is measured on its own airframe. There is no Embraer evidence in my record: following Culp and doctrine. GEnx is measured against the baseline GEnx fleet on the GE90/GEnx architecture [CX-0169]. Every finding goes to a cross-functional team [CX-0012]. Any finding touching both aircraft goes to the Board at once. We fix the part [CX-0005]. Flag (ask 2): none on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx, because no finding is in front of me. That is not a clearance.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years between the Ducted's ready year and each new narrowbody's entry. A defensive Ducted earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036: 1 year ahead of NGSA (2037) and 4 ahead of fps (2040). Reconciliation, from the board's arithmetic and not a test (inference). I can match the observed share in every year only without the Ducted's +10. 2037: Boeing 39 on the 737 slot (CFM) + Airbus 61/3 = 59.33; + Embraer 5 - Joint Venture 10 = 54.33, over 105 = 51.7% (observed 51.7). 2038: 51.1 (observed 51.1). 2039: 50.5 (observed 50.5). From 2040: 33.33 + 5 - 10 = 28.33, over 105 = 27.0% (observed 27.0). With the Ducted's +10 added, these would be 61.3, 60.6, 60.0 and 36.5%. So the brief does not show 'its +10 pp NB counting' since the Joint Venture formed. I don't know the board's reason. It changes no order, because the Ducted can only be held. But neither the Board nor the public should hear a share claim for the Ducted. Its case is durability and support, which is the frame anyway.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, Rows B and C and the 2050 forward look (advice; Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: The Open Fan must be ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry, or the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap. Not a veto ground, because the ready year itself is correct (inference).
tests.numbers: Confirmed, all three. (1) A 2045 launch is ready in 2055: 18 years after NGSA (2037) and 15 after fps (2040). H2 binds in S1, the only column. (2) A 2050 launch is ready in 2060: 23 and 20 years late. (3) 'Launched and ready by 2050' is out of reach by any order, since 2055 is after 2050. Rows against hold in S1: Row B Open Fan -26.27 (-95.96); Row C Open Fan + Lobby -21.89 (-91.58). The dollars are Ghai's; the gap in years is mine. Culp's plan holds the Open Fan, so no order he leans to fails.

tests.name: RISE gates, reported as the state of the technology (Culp's ask 5)
tests.threshold: (1) Flight test; (2) compact-core durability turned on and turned off; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. This is the state of the technology, not a product case, and not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Reported back against the promise. Nothing new since last round's report: neither the brief nor the bulletin carries a RISE test result, and my record ends in October 2025. (1) Flight test: not shown. The fly demo was promised 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0001, CX-0151] and moved to 'this decade' [CX-0211], and no result is on the record. (2) Compact core: HPT-blade dust testing began in October 2025 [CX-0222], with over 350 programme tests and an early focus on durability [CX-0216]. No turn-off result. (3) More than 20%: the design figure [CX-0001] and the physics case [CX-0180], not shown in engine test. (4) Noise: shown as a capability with Airbus [CX-0013], not on a product engine. Count: three gates not closed, one shown in part. No RISE date is promised. With no Open Fan order, this informs the Board and blocks nothing.

tests.name: Physics
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is company doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Wording check (inference).
tests.numbers: Culp's red line is at least 20% [CX-0217]. RISE: 'more than 20%' as design [CX-0001]; 'practically impossible ... without the open fan' [CX-0180]. Ducted: 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183]. The frame and draft line call only RISE the next generation and give no fuel-burn number. Pass. A public RISE fuel-burn number would need an engine test, and the record shows none.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: No durability data is in the brief. Hold everything trades nothing: there is no new programme and no schedule to protect. The draft line commits to earning the record and claims no result. Flag: none. That is not a clearance; see the fleet durability report.

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers: recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only).
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project. The $2B strain is already in the hold row (-2.00 of -69.69). Row C adds Lobby and, on the Board's reading, $2B more of strain on a row the grid does not pay. There is no evidence in my record on running the supply chain: following doctrine (the strain rule) and Culp's data [CX-0613]. Data for the re-based joint plan (S1, brief): CFM NB engines a year: 3,040 to 2036; 2,070 (2037), 2,044 (2038), 2,019 (2039); 1,079 from 2040 to 2056. That is 35.5% of the 2036 rate, a 64.5% cut. WB: 143, then 152 from 2042. The 737 slot flew LEAP-1B until fps entered in 2040 (rules). The load moves from OE to the aftermarket: the LEAP fleet built at up to 3,040 a year, the Ducted's first shop visits on NGSA (since 2037) and fps (since 2040), GE9X and the durability kits, all behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. The brief has no supplier field data (shortages, misses, quality escapes), so I give no supply 'no', and no 'yes' on test. Doctrine: OE before spares [CX-0529]. Parts needed to clear an inspection finding on a safety-critical part go first, ahead of both, because safety comes first (inference) [CX-0658, CX-0010]. No new facility, and lean before capital. Take Culp's quarter-to-half haircut off the shop-visit ramp as well as any OE promise [CX-0590, CX-0592]. Jointly with Safran, with no number in public. Money, booking and capex: No evidence: following Ghai.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture over a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into in-service upgrades while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: The hold keeps the GEnx upgrade on the GE90/GEnx architecture, counting since 2042 [CX-0169]. RISE technology goes into the LEAP and Ducted fleets as upgrades only where turn-on, turn-off testing supports it [CX-0162, CX-0009]. Any field finding on the Ducted is fixed at the part, not by redesigning or cancelling the engine [CX-0005].

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem in the brief or an order touches safety or durability, it needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: No problem in the brief touches safety. In-service durability is now the work. Culp's other move (1) and the Board's first recommendation make every fleet finding a cross-functional call, and any finding touching both aircraft goes to the Board at once. 'No single person can make a safety decision.'

tests.name: Partner Embraer date
tests.threshold: Embraer counts 7 years after launch and needs a new CFM engine. Its count year must not come before that engine's ready year (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched 2030, counts 2037 (2030 + 7), on the Ducted ready 2036. It can only be held. There is no Embraer evidence in my record: following Culp and doctrine. State no Embraer date or durability figure in public.

tests.name: GEnx date, and the off-grid WB dates (Culp's ask 3)
tests.threshold: GEnx counts 3 years after launch, from the first Re-engine's entry or 2042 (inference). Rival WB dates checked against the public rules only.
tests.numbers: GEnx: launched 2030, ready 2033, counting since 2042 (WB 44.8% in the brief). No date issue. No Re-engine is on the record. Boeing: debt first and one step at a time. Airbus: one programme at a time. RR: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and its Trent time-on-wing work is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order. A Re-engine does not move the GEnx count year, which has already started. Culp's off-grid dates check out on the rules: a Trent 1000 upgrade launched in 2045 counts from 2048 (+3). An UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051 (+6) and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service, earliest 2050 (a 2045 Re-engine + 5), so it counts from 2051. Their dollars are Ghai's.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone (Row B) or with Lobby (Row C), now or in the 2050 round; and lobby_emissions: launch on its own
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a date veto. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 (launch + 10, after the 2045 floor), and a 2050 launch in 2060. Neither is earlier than the development time, so my binding date ground does not fail them. They fail ready-no-later-than-the-airframe: 18 years late against NGSA (2037) and 15 against fps (2040), losing the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Against hold in S1: Row B -26.27, Row C -21.89. No RISE gate is closed on the record: no flight test, no compact-core turn-off, and no 20% in engine test. A RISE product would have nothing on test behind it. Lobby alone does nothing without a live Open Fan. My record is silent on lobbying: following Culp and doctrine.

vetoes.plan: Pre-notice for step 4, not an objection to Culp's lean. A public statement or other move that gives a Ducted, Embraer or GEnx time-on-wing, cycle, shop-visit or durability claim the field data has not earned (including 'proven durability', 'mature time on wing' or CFM56 parity), an Open Fan entry or ready year, a RISE flight-test year, a RISE fuel-burn figure stated as a result, a capacity or rate number or ramp date, or a claim that the Ducted holds NB share.
vetoes.ground: Binding ground 2 (a public date or claim no real test backs). The brief carries no field data on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx, no RISE flight test and no engine-test fuel burn. Nothing is vetoed now. If the step-4 statement carries such a claim, I veto it then, and the veto binds unless Culp answers it with test or field evidence. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results; the team rule and the GM read them as a binding date test.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test or field data only, never analysis. (1) A Ducted or Embraer field finding: unscheduled removals clustering on a few part numbers, distress in hot and harsh, a life-limited-part finding at inspection, or time on wing falling short of the CFM56 in the same environment. I would raise a durability flag, take it to a cross-functional team and the Board at once, turn it on and turn it off in test, and fix the part, not redesign or cancel the engine. (2) Supplier field data: shortages or quality escapes concentrating again in the 9 suppliers at 15 sites, or shop-visit turn times or OE deliveries missing on them. I would then give a supply 'no' to any added work and cut the private capacity commitment. (3) RISE: flight test done, the compact core turned on and turned off, more than 20% shown in engine test. That would change the state of the technology but not this round's Open Fan call, because both new narrowbodies are in service long before 2055; the gap is the airframe, not the test. (4) The board's own numbers showing the Ducted's +10 pp counting would close my reconciliation note; it changes no order either way. (5) A Re-engine on the record would put the rival WB dates (2048, 2051) in play; GEnx's count year stays 2042.
ops.memo:
Larry, testing, not analysis.

Dates. Every order passes. Ducted: 2030 plus 6 is 2036, a year ahead of NGSA, four ahead of fps. Embraer counts 2037. GEnx ready 2033, counting since 2042; no Re-engine on the record. Open Fan launched now is ready 2055: 18 years after NGSA, 15 after fps. Launched in 2050, 2060. 'Ready by 2050' is out of reach by any order.

Fleet durability. The brief carries no field data. No time on wing, no shop visits, no life-limited parts at full life, no inspection findings. Analysis does not fill it. What I bring the Board: fleet-leader and fleet-average cycles to first shop visit, by aircraft and environment, hot and harsh separate, against the CFM56 in the same environment, as with LEAP; removal causes by part; life-limited-part findings; every distress turned on and turned off in test. Embraer measured on its own. Every finding a cross-functional call. We fix the part.

Flag: none, because nothing is in front of me. That is not a clearance.

One admission. I reconcile 27.0% only without the Ducted's +10. Claim no share for it.

RISE: nothing new. Flight test not shown. Dust testing started, no turn-off. 20% is physics and design, not engine test. Lower noise than LEAP shown as a capability. Technology, no date.

Supply. Hold adds nothing. NB OE falls from 3,040 to 1,079 a year; the load moves to shop visits on the same nine suppliers. Haircut that ramp too.

Your line passes. Hold everything. No veto.

other_moves.move: Fleet durability report to the full Board: the Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade
Joint CFM capacity plan re-based with Safran to the volume we actually have
other_moves.detail:
This is a private planning basis built through CFM governance. It is not a commitment to anyone [CX-0184, CX-0944].
- The basis is the board's volume of 1,079 CFM NB engines a year from 2040. That is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year built to 2036. WB is 152 a year from 2042.
- 1,079 is the board's volume, not an airframer's agreed schedule. No capacity or rate number goes to an airframer or the public until that airframer's volumes are worked.
- The risk now is stranded capacity, not a missed ramp. So we build no new facility: lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue and goes to MRO turnaround on the fleet we have, not to OE lines.
- Priority: parts needed to clear a finding on a safety-critical part come first [CX-0658, CX-0010]; then OE engines ahead of spares [CX-0529].
- The load moves to the aftermarket: the LEAP fleet, the Ducted's first shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, all behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. I take a quarter to a half off any shop-visit ramp promise as well as any OE promise [CX-0590, CX-0592].

other_moves.move: Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx fleets, on standard terms
Keep RISE funded as technology, and report its gates as the state of the technology
CFM parity record for a hold

Fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice: both airframers fly CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are flying, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on the next order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job now is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines arrive on time for our customers' deliveries first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at hold. That is the default (Do Nothing), so no order is a Board item.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
The narrowbody selections are settled. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both in service on code 7, so the codes are locked. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and its engine has been ready since 2036. No order on this menu buys back a point of NB share.

So the game is the installed base we have:
- 1,079 CFM NB engines a year on two aircraft we share three ways;
- the LEAP fleet behind them;
- 152 GEnx a year from 2042.
"Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422].

We win it on execution, in this order: safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. That means:
- durability earned in the field, not on analysis [CX-0009];
- OE ahead of spares [CX-0529];
- support that earns the next order, with no birthright [CX-0564];
- RISE kept whole as technology [CX-0214, CX-0469].

GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1, rivals hold: the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column)
- Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan, 0.00 against Do Nothing.
- Open Fan: -95.96, which is -26.27 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus an $18.27B wait penalty: CFM's 27% NB share goes to zero for 2045-2056. My check is $18.28B on 1,079 engines a year.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -91.58, which is -21.89 against hold. Ghai reconciles it: a $9B bill ($8B + $1B) plus $12.89B of NB value lost. With Lobby, CFM keeps 7.9% rather than 0%. The grid charges no second $2B strain, so I adopt his correction of my frame and the Board's $11B. Lobby is worth +4.38 inside the row, and only against a penalty the Open Fan creates.
- Lobby alone is not on the grid. It is -1.00 for no board effect (Ghai), not $3B as my frame allowed.
- Tie-break: not needed. The smallest gap to hold is $21.89B, far outside ε.

TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk: no row beats hold. S1 is the only column, so no choice of weights changes this.
- Low case first: S1 is the public record. I book below it at -71.
- H2, the airframer sets the date: a 2045 Open Fan is ready in 2055. That is 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's, so it waits in the only column. Ali confirms the dates. The one exception, the RISE allowance, would need $21.89B against a $15B cap. Not used.
- H3: the Ducted was the defence the rule calls for, and it is in service. I make no new claim for it, and I never call it the next generation.
- My 20% line binds RISE only. None of Ali's RISE gates is closed on the record.
- Durability line [CX-0208]: a hold trades nothing. The fleet durability report is how I enforce it now.
- H5: RISE stays funded, with no cancel and no program dividend. H8: the statement names no rival, the Joint Venture included, and blames no one.
- H9: premium $0.

A CORRECTION TO MY FRAME (Ali's reconciliation)
My frame said the Ducted had 'its +10 pp NB counting'. Ali shows that the observed shares reconcile only without it:
- 2040: 33.33 + 5 (Embraer) - 10 (Joint Venture) = 28.33 over 105, which is 27.0%, matching the bulletin;
- with the Ducted's +10 it would be 36.5%.
I checked his arithmetic and it holds for 2037-2040. I don't know the board's reason. It changes no order, because the Ducted can only be held. It does change what we say: we claim no NB share for the Ducted, in public or to the Board. Its case is durability and support. If the board's numbers ever show the +10, that is upside, and it is not booked.

FORWARD LOOK (2050, the last round)
- Open Fan: -17.05 against hold.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -15.39, ready in 2060, after the NB window closes in 2056 (Ghai's figures, which match mine).
The second is $0.39B over the allowance, but that is not the point. It would wait in the only column, so H2 binds and the Board vetoes it. It could not meet 'ready by 2050' either. We don't revisit it on hope.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
There is no new CFM narrowbody order. Fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice: both airframers fly CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. No Safran position is asserted. GEnx is GE alone.

EXCO
Both memos recommend all-hold. Every binding test passes, so there are no overrides.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THREE THINGS:
- the Embraer hold (profile §6; my record is silent on Embraer);
- the Lobby rule;
- the supply-load read (the strain rule, with my ramp haircut applied to shop visits too, since Ali has no supplier field data).

CAPITAL
- No new R&D. The 70% payout and the A-range rating are whole [CX-0645].
- No new facility. Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue and goes to MRO turnaround.
- Booking: -71. Hold at -69.69 less the larger of two mutually exclusive off-grid WB exposures ($1.13B), rounded down. That raises last round's -77 now that the codes have locked, as we said we would [CX-0654].

- RISE gates: nothing new. Flight test not shown, no compact-core turn-off, 20% only in design and physics, noise shown as a capability. That is the state of the technology.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are flying, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on the next order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job now is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines arrive on time for our customers' deliveries first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

vetoes.plan: Public statement and other moves. CONDITIONAL, not invoked as drafted

I invoke it if the statement or any other move does any of the following: claims time on wing beyond the hours flown; calls Joint Venture engine durability 'proven' before the fleet data show it; claims the credibility objective; presents lifecycle value ($13.2B against $8.7B) as cash or free cash flow; or announces or books value from a merged derivative, UltraFan NB content or the 2050 round. The draft as framed passes. Acceptable alternative: say less.

vetoes.plan: Draft public statement, capital line ('debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels')
vetoes.ground: None of my four grounds; advice. The board models no debt path, and the analyst models stop at 2030E. Write it as an order of priority ('dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks'), not as a status we can evidence in 2045. Likewise, 'never takes parts or engineers from the fleet' is Eddy's to evidence; if he cannot, it should say less.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: The order cannot change: both fields offer only hold. What would change my numbers or my advice: (1) A revised brief offering a Board item, such as a Joint Venture cash call, top-up, merged derivative or UltraFan NB content. That is a new appropriation through my gate and Finance. It needs a return case against hold and a buyback, the dividend whole and debt on its pre-ASR path, and its own durability programme; booked $0 until on the record. (2) Eddy's fleet data showing a durability shortfall, a fix or retrofit campaign, or parts drawn from the GTF fleet. I book that downside fast, with contingency before the estimate and a dated follow-up, and the statement says less. (3) Evidence that the step-up to 1,460 engines a year carries a negative engine margin deep enough to strain near-term cash. That would not move ΔPV, but it would move my cash-by-year view and the buyback fill-in. (4) A 2050 brief with a column other than S1. I would weight it and book nothing before the record.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. One row, one column: 'GTF2: hold' at +8.88 (108.1%) in S1. Expected, worst and booked are the same number, all on the public record: formed in 2035, ready since 2036, fitted on NGSA and fps. S1 = 1.00.

Hold and hold. Neither is a capital order or a Board item, and none of my four grounds reaches them. A fitted engine is not an unselected one.

No new money. No R&D and no write-off since 2035. The fold write-off was $0, and I release my $2B contingency. GTF2 cost its plan: $2.00B, about $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the envelope. The board moved that line from 2030 to 2035; undiscounted, so value is unchanged. The Joint Venture has asked for nothing beyond that $2B. Anything more is a new appropriation through my gate and Finance, against hold and a buyback.

What I worry about: $13.2B against $8.7B is lifecycle value, not cash. Five hundred more engines a year, likely at a negative engine margin, cost cash first and pay back over 20-25 years of shop visits, as the V2500 did. I will not call it free cash flow.

Capital order unchanged: dividend, then debt back to pre-ASR, then buybacks. Past 2030 that rests on board numbers alone.

On S4, I had it at 0.08, and I was wrong. Rolls-Royce held the same free option we did. We were right because the order was dominant, not because I read them well. Booking zero was right.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSAL (Eddy, operating seat; Calio decides): gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only values the brief lists (§3). The grid row is 'GTF2: hold', +8.88 (108.1%) in S1, its only column. Neither order is a Board item.
- gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and the engine has been ready since 2036. An engine can be cancelled only until it is ready, so that window is closed. No live airframe is waiting to enter service, so neither launch value can be ordered. My lever rule says hold once GTF2 is live or no airframe can use it in time, and both now apply.
- jv_with_rr: hold. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation. My conditions for proposing withdraw do not apply either: the engine was ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS and fps's 2040 EIS, and nothing on the record hands over the gear or the core.

ANSWERS TO CALIO
1. Veto status. Ground 1 (durability not proven before EIS): pass. No order and no line in your draft puts an engine on an airframe before it is ready or claims durability. Ground 2 (parts and capacity short of the fleet's needs): pass on the board, because there is no launch and no live problem is shown. I invoke neither. Both passes rest on the board, not on data.
2. In-service record of the Joint Venture engine.
- Severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs before each EIS: I can't evidence either. The board's 'ready 2036' is launch + 6, a schedule rule, not a test result. The only outside read: Airbus said each engine joins 'once its maturity and durability are proven', Boeing said the others 'follow on their durability evidence', and both fitted P&W. That is the customers' read, not our data.
- Fleet hours: I don't have them. The board gives deliveries only. P&W delivered 10,233 NB engines in 2037-44 (965 + 978 + 990 + 5 x 1,460), and the board does not split the Joint Venture engine from GTF.
- By analogy (inference, not for public use): the GTF passed 1M hours by November 2018, within about 3 years of entering service and at far lower volume [P-0328][P-0895]. So NGSA is likely past the benchmark. The bad news is that the benchmark surfaces problems; it does not prove durability. The hot-and-sandy time-on-wing shortfall [PX-0122] and the 2023 recall [PX-0290] both came after the GTF passed 1M hours.
- Fix campaigns: none is on the record, and the board carries none, so I cannot say there were none. My prior is 2-3 campaigns in years 1-5, each taking about 2 years to run through the fleet [P-0895]. NGSA is in year 8 of service and fps in year 5.
3. GTF fleet.
- I have no 2045 AOG count, no pacing-parts count and no kit-insertion progress.
- Last data: 10% AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120]; an average of about 350 AOG forecast for 2024-26, with a 600-650 peak [P-1039]; about 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]. The kit carries 90-95% of the Advantage's gains [P-0786] and is charged [P-1363].
- The rule that AOG recovery gets first call on parts was written into the 2035 sealed orders. Whether it held is not in evidence.
4. Capacity.
- The step from 990 engines (2039) to 1,460 (2040) is +470, or +47.5% in one year, and +52% against the status quo's 960.
- I cannot confirm that it drew no castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from fleet support. Nor can I confirm that new capacity was qualified before it shipped. The rule was written; the outcome is not in evidence.
- A flat 36.5% share in 2040-44 shows no delivery shortfall on the board, but the board does not model parts.
- This step matches our past escapes: the 2015 HMI powder tower added for the ramp [P-1040], and the 2019 and 2024 ramps [P-1062].
- Contain first (inference): run a records look-back on parts from capacity added for the 2040 step. The powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039].
- Pacing parts at 1,460: structural castings [PX-0125], forgings and powder-metal disks, inside the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]. No count at the 1,460 rate is in evidence. The trade-off is the one I described in 2023: new engines against the MRO shops [PX-0123][PX-0124].
5. The 2035 Board ask cannot be evidenced. Our sealed 2035 orders said the first count comes 'with the next package'. The Board asked for a cadence before NGSA's EIS only after the orders were sealed. My veto-check advice (a weekly drumbeat to ExCo) was advice, not an order, and nothing in the run record shows what reached the Committee. From here: a standing report, weekly to ExCo [PX-0131] and quarterly to the Governance and Public Policy Committee (the quarterly cadence is my inference), and at once on any escape. It covers:
- fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122] against about 1M hours;
- removals and time on wing against plan;
- AOG for both fleets;
- the pacing-parts count;
- kit insertion as a % of the fleet [PX-0116];
- capacity qualification status;
- any escape, with its containment and a dated recovery.
6. Joint Venture governance.
- On the record, yes. The 2035 public terms keep the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology as P&W modules under P&W design authority, and nothing in the 2045 bulletin changes them. The Joint Venture contract itself is not on the board. Design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240].
- Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim [P-2004] stays closed only while P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data.
- Pressure point: Rolls-Royce's 2035 public move said its technology 'comes into' the Joint Venture. On an in-service engine, any Rolls-Royce content is a configuration change. It needs a new appropriation and its own durability programme, and it should not happen while the in-service record is still being earned.
- One engine is confirmed: UltraFan NB never entered service. How the support chain is split between P&W, Rolls-Royce and partners is not on the record.
7. Engineering load: no new development. The load is in-service support: one engine on two airframes, plus the GTF fleet and the kit. Two airframes can bring airframe-specific findings (inference). This is advice; the board has no strain charge, and I have no team data.
8. 2050: nothing technical on the grid changes hold. Three things are in view: the fps fix-campaign window, Rolls-Royce's push for content, and the 2040 capacity look-back. Each is a fleet matter for other moves and the Committee, not an order.

OTHER MOVES: (i) to (vi) pass my grounds. I add the records look-back to (ii). One wording fix for the statement: 'never takes parts or engineers' states a 2040-45 fact I cannot evidence, so write it as the rule: 'may not take'. 'We have learned our lesson' is a claim; the data will show whether it holds (advice). The statement carries no fleet figure, because I have none.

My record is one event, June 2023, before the recall. Joint Venture, capacity and Committee views are seat doctrine and inference.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view on any of the following.
- Fleet data showing a durability shortfall on the Joint Venture engine (removals, short time on wing in hot-and-harsh operation, a fix campaign): fleet first, a dated recovery, and a Committee report at once. If parts are short, I invoke ground 2 against the rate.
- An escape, or a finding from the 2040 capacity look-back: contain first, before any new commitment.
- A proposal to put UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative into the in-service engine without its own durability programme, or a public 'proven' claim before the data: I invoke ground 1.
- Joint Venture terms that move the gear or core: I flag the red line.
- A revised 2050 brief that offers a Board item: I re-run readiness against each live airframe's EIS before proposing anything other than hold.
ops.memo:
Bad number first: I don't have one. The board carries no fleet hours, no AOG count, no pacing-parts count and no time-on-wing figure for either engine fleet. My last data are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet waiting on engines, about 30 pacing parts. My parts passes in 2030 and 2035 rested on the board. So does today's.

What is on the record: the engine, GTF2 by the fold, was ready in 2036, one year ahead of NGSA and four ahead of fps. Both airframers said they would fit only on durability evidence, and both fitted us. That's their read, not our data.

I can't evidence that any count reached the Governance Committee before NGSA's entry into service. Our 2035 orders said "with the next package". That's on us. From here: a standing report, weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee.

Two things worry me. The 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year was 47% in one year, and our last escape came from capacity added for a ramp. I want a records review of every part made on that new capacity. And a million hours surfaces problems; it doesn't prove durability. The GTF passed it in 2018. The hot-and-sandy time on wing and the recall came later.

Orders: hold and hold, the only legal values. Neither of my grounds is triggered. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay ours.

My record is one investor day, before the recall. The rest is seat doctrine.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. An engine earns its durability record one flight hour at a time, and our new engine's record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. So we will report time on wing as fleet data, and we will claim nothing beyond the hours flown. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The fleet data will show whether we have, not this statement.

Here is what is on the record. The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners committed. What we said then, that nothing had formed, no longer stands. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine. Any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week. Our rule is that new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates or rates, or for Rolls-Royce. Those are theirs to announce.
decision.rationale:
CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00.

NO BOARD ITEM IS AVAILABLE, AND WHY
- The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready.
- A withdraw is illegal, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and withdraw is legal only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected cannot be ordered, because no live airframe is waiting to enter service: both new narrowbodies are in service.
- So the 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test written in 2035 (Eddy's condition d, Mitchill's three-part rule) has nothing left to decide. The Board's request to align it with the Premature exit test is moot for the same reason. For the record, its lapse conditions are checked and none has lapsed:
  - code 7 includes Rolls-Royce on both airframes;
  - nothing is billed beyond $2B;
  - P&W is not trimmed (36.5% each);
  - the modules are kept.
- Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles are taken.

DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
- I start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold.
- Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds on either order. A fitted engine is not an unselected one, and the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: no order puts an engine on an airframe, and the brief shows no live fleet problem.
- Conditional vetoes, all respected:
  - Mitchill ground 4: no time-on-wing or 'proven' claim, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative or 2050 value.
  - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged; no concessions.
  - Eddy grounds 1 and 2: no configuration change without its own durability programme; the fleet ring-fence and qualified capacity.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through other moves, not orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the 1,460 rate waits if the weekly review shows the fleet short.
- Overrides: none.

PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE
- premium_b 0. Hold/hold is the only and best plan.
- The cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap (the round-1 doctrine premium; $0.34B at Mitchill's weights).
- Both objectives are met on the board, with $0 of PV given up.

WHOLE-PROGRAMME VALUE AGAINST PLAN (for the Board, P-1191; Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own)
- 2030: launch_if_selected fired on code 7. Expected PV was +0.23 at my weights and -1.72 at Mitchill's; booked 0.00. That grid's both-select-us column (S5) read +22.00, but it assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine. Rolls-Royce launched UltraFan NB in 2030 and both airframes took code 7, so by 2035 hold read +3.37.
- 2035 grid:
  - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37;
  - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88.
  - Expected: +0.39 (mine), +0.07 (Mitchill's). Booked: +3.37.
- Outcome: +8.88, the S4 column. The commit added +5.51 over hold.
- Measures:
  - +8.81 over Mitchill's 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected;
  - 13.12 below the 2030 S5 column;
  - return of $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.4x;
  - board-basis payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal, 2041 discounted to 2026. Cash payback is later and not on the board.
- Cost against plan: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope (Mitchill's phasing, not board data). The brief now shows the $2.0B in 2035 rather than 2030. It is the same undiscounted $2.00B booked once, so no value changes. The fold write-off was $0. Mitchill's $2B contingency is released. The Joint Venture asked for no P&W cash beyond the $2B. No new R&D and no write-off this round.

WHAT I OWN
(1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (Mitchill's). In a sealed, simultaneous round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free and as dominant for it as ours was for us. We should have weighted it that way. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well. The lesson for sealed rounds: when a rival's order is free and conditional, weight it as likely.
(2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan. It assumed a market without a Rolls-Royce narrowbody engine.
(3) The Board's 2035 tightening of the statement was not taken up. We published 'GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change', which could be read as a promise of 2036. The 2036 date held on the board. That is counter-evidence to my optimism on dates, not a licence: I state no new date this year.
(4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced. Our 2035 orders said 'with the next package'. That is on us. It is replaced from today by a standing cadence: weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, at once on any escape.
(5) Eddy has no fleet data: no hours, AOG, pacing-parts count or kit progress. His parts passes in 2030, 2035 and today rest on the board. So the statement says less, and makes no durability or time-on-wing claim.
(6) The 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year was +47.5% in one year, and our last escape came from ramp capacity. I order the records look-back as containment, not as a finding.

CAPITAL: dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks.
- Analyst context to 2030E only (Mitchill): the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, with debt back to pre-ASR levels by about 2028-30E (his approximation, inference). Buybacks are the fill-in at $4.0-5.0B a year.
- Past 2030, this rests on board numbers alone.
- The $13.2B against $8.7B (2045, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow.

BIAS CHECK
- Optimism on dates: none stated.
- Architecture loyalty: the Joint Venture engine is GTF2. The test now is the time-on-wing record, not loyalty. Any Rolls-Royce content is a configuration change and needs its own appropriation and durability programme.
- Value capture: the kit stays charged.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: the Joint Venture governance positions [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004] and the Committee cadence are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference. My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low).

2050: unless that brief prices a Board item, hold. Any merged derivative, UltraFan NB content or cash call comes through the gate, and nothing is booked before the record.

final.public_statement:
Bad news first. An engine earns its durability record one flight hour at a time, and our new engine's record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. So we will report time on wing as fleet data, and we will claim nothing beyond the hours flown. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The fleet data will show whether we have, not this statement.

Here is what is on the record. The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners committed. What we said then, that nothing had formed, no longer stands. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine. Any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week. Our rule is that new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates or rates, or for Rolls-Royce. Those are theirs to announce.
final.rationale:
CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00.

NO BOARD ITEM IS AVAILABLE, AND WHY
- The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready.
- A withdraw is illegal, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and withdraw is legal only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected cannot be ordered, because no live airframe is waiting to enter service: both new narrowbodies are in service.
- So the 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test written in 2035 (Eddy's condition d, Mitchill's three-part rule) has nothing left to decide. The Board's request to align it with the Premature exit test is moot for the same reason. For the record, its lapse conditions are checked and none has lapsed:
  - code 7 includes Rolls-Royce on both airframes;
  - nothing is billed beyond $2B;
  - P&W is not trimmed (36.5% each);
  - the modules are kept.
- Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles are taken.

DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
- I start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold.
- Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds on either order. A fitted engine is not an unselected one, and the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: no order puts an engine on an airframe, and the brief shows no live fleet problem.
- Conditional vetoes, all respected:
  - Mitchill ground 4: no time-on-wing or 'proven' claim, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative or 2050 value.
  - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged; no concessions.
  - Eddy grounds 1 and 2: no configuration change without its own durability programme; the fleet ring-fence and qualified capacity.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through other moves, not orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the 1,460 rate waits if the weekly review shows the fleet short.
- Overrides: none.

PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE
- premium_b 0. Hold/hold is the only and best plan.
- The cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap (the round-1 doctrine premium; $0.34B at Mitchill's weights).
- Both objectives are met on the board, with $0 of PV given up.

WHOLE-PROGRAMME VALUE AGAINST PLAN (for the Board, P-1191; Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own)
- 2030: launch_if_selected fired on code 7. Expected PV was +0.23 at my weights and -1.72 at Mitchill's; booked 0.00. That grid's both-select-us column (S5) read +22.00, but it assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine. Rolls-Royce launched UltraFan NB in 2030 and both airframes took code 7, so by 2035 hold read +3.37.
- 2035 grid:
  - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37;
  - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88.
  - Expected: +0.39 (mine), +0.07 (Mitchill's). Booked: +3.37.
- Outcome: +8.88, the S4 column. The commit added +5.51 over hold.
- Measures:
  - +8.81 over Mitchill's 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected;
  - 13.12 below the 2030 S5 column;
  - return of $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.4x;
  - board-basis payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal, 2041 discounted to 2026. Cash payback is later and not on the board.
- Cost against plan: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope (Mitchill's phasing, not board data). The brief now shows the $2.0B in 2035 rather than 2030. It is the same undiscounted $2.00B booked once, so no value changes. The fold write-off was $0. Mitchill's $2B contingency is released. The Joint Venture asked for no P&W cash beyond the $2B. No new R&D and no write-off this round.

WHAT I OWN
(1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (Mitchill's). In a sealed, simultaneous round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free and as dominant for it as ours was for us. We should have weighted it that way. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well. The lesson for sealed rounds: when a rival's order is free and conditional, weight it as likely.
(2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan. It assumed a market without a Rolls-Royce narrowbody engine.
(3) The Board's 2035 tightening of the statement was not taken up. We published 'GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change', which could be read as a promise of 2036. The 2036 date held on the board. That is counter-evidence to my optimism on dates, not a licence: I state no new date this year.
(4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced. Our 2035 orders said 'with the next package'. That is on us. It is replaced from today by a standing cadence: weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, at once on any escape.
(5) Eddy has no fleet data: no hours, AOG, pacing-parts count or kit progress. His parts passes in 2030, 2035 and today rest on the board. So the statement says less, and makes no durability or time-on-wing claim.
(6) The 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year was +47.5% in one year, and our last escape came from ramp capacity. I order the records look-back as containment, not as a finding.

CAPITAL: dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks.
- Analyst context to 2030E only (Mitchill): the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, with debt back to pre-ASR levels by about 2028-30E (his approximation, inference). Buybacks are the fill-in at $4.0-5.0B a year.
- Past 2030, this rests on board numbers alone.
- The $13.2B against $8.7B (2045, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow.

BIAS CHECK
- Optimism on dates: none stated.
- Architecture loyalty: the Joint Venture engine is GTF2. The test now is the time-on-wing record, not loyalty. Any Rolls-Royce content is a configuration change and needs its own appropriation and durability programme.
- Value capture: the kit stays charged.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: the Joint Venture governance positions [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004] and the Committee cadence are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference. My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low).

2050: unless that brief prices a Board item, hold. Any merged derivative, UltraFan NB content or cash call comes through the gate, and nothing is booked before the record.

recommendations.text: Defend the widebody core inside the existing budget. Hold both widebody orders this round. Continue Trent time on wing as an unpriced other move: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Our order holds: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp runs over, buybacks give way first, as in 2015. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes to the board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.

Control's terms and the forward plan. State plainly that our own narrowbody money is $5.71B against $4B, and that it is final: the $4B share plus the $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. No narrowbody order remains open to change it. The cause was the 2030 double selection; we never cancel for the metric. The line still in our hands is strain, at $0. Last round's 2045 withdraw plan is closed, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035. When we commit, we deliver, and we did.

Public statement and other moves. Say plainly that the Joint Venture formed and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies, and that the fleet comes first. Give no date for any new programme and say nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates. Describe no venture terms beyond the record. Keep both airframers on standard commercial terms, through the Investment Committee, with no concessions to hold a position. On widebody, say 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody; Trent time on wing keeps improving'.
