tests.threshold: Durability before long-dated programmes. State when each order starts to earn (inference)
tests.numbers:
- Hold: the Joint Venture engine has earned since 2037 (NGSA) and 2040 (fps).
- Upgrade: counts from 2048, 3 years after launch. It earns about +0.53 in all and never repays its $2B bill.
- UltraFan WB: ready in 2051, and it counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. None is on the record. In S2-S3 it earns +0.73 to +0.98 against $4B.

tests.name: Premium (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Price every doctrine or objective premium in $B. Above $3B a round (above $1B for UltraFan WB), the PV-best order applies
tests.numbers:
- $0 at hold, item by item. Hold is the best grid plan in every column. Confirmed.
- The upgrade would need a $6.47B premium, above the $3B cap.
- UltraFan WB would need $8.83B on expectation, above its $1B sub-cap.
- Neither can be carried.

tests.name: Control: own narrowbody money within $4B
tests.threshold: Own NB development money, committed or written off, at or below $4B (scored by Control; never changes the payoff)
tests.numbers:
- $5.71B in every column: the $4B share plus $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. The figure is final.
- No order is open on either narrowbody field.
- The cause was the 2030 double selection. We never cancel or fold for the metric. Stated plainly.

tests.name: Control: strain, widebody dominance and narrowbody entry (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Strain $0; RR WB engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050; RR NB share above 0 in 2045 and 2050
tests.numbers:
Hold (own NB money / strain / RR WB share 2050 / RR NB share 2050 / Airbus WB airframe share):
- S1: $5.7B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% / 41.2%.
- S2: $5.7B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% / 40.2%.
- S3: $5.7B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% / 41.2%.
Confirmed. Strain is the one line still in our hands. Either widebody launch would move it from $0 to $5B for good. The upgrade would lift widebody share to 60.0%, but dominance is already met at 55.2%.

tests.name: 2050 test in advance (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: The same tests next round: each row against "UltraFan NB: hold", column by column, in the last round (inference)
tests.numbers:
- Upgrade launched in 2050. It counts from 2053 and carries its $2B bill plus the permanent $5B strain. To pass the worst-case test it must be no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column, which needs about +$5B of engine value. To sit within the $3B premium cap it needs about +$4B; to beat hold outright, about +$7B. A 2045 launch earns about +0.53, and a 2050 launch would earn less, over fewer years to 2061. On this board a Re-engine does not change the upgrade's value: the row's gap to hold is the same -6.47 in every column. I expect it to fail.
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050. It is ready in 2056 and counts only once a Re-engine is in service. It qualifies only if an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, is on the record. The binding bar is the $1B sub-cap: within $1.00B of hold in every plausible column. That needs about +$8B of engine value, against +0.73 to +0.98 today. I expect it to fail.
- If a Re-engine goes on the record this round, bring both rows and I will re-run them. I expect hold.

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch
vetoes.ground: Hurdle and downside. "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade" is -6.47 against hold in every column, so -6.47 under any weights. Its worst column, -6.47, is 3.2x its own $2B bill, with the $5B strain inside the row. The shortfall exceeds the $3B premium cap. Even without the strain it is -1.47. I withhold my co-signature.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch
vetoes.ground: Hurdle and downside. "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB" is -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02 against hold, -8.83 at both the CEO's and the Board's weights. Its worst column, -9.00, is 2.25x its own $4B bill. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and the shortfall is far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. I withhold my co-signature.

vetoes.plan: Balance-sheet vetoes (equity raise, leverage above about 1.5x, levering up for buybacks)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. At hold no new money is committed. The ramp and any shared retrofit are met from free cash flow, and buybacks give way first. Board debt of $40B on an EV of $110B is unchanged.

vetoes.plan: Other moves: Rolls-Royce money beyond the $4B Joint Venture share, or any concession to hold a position
vetoes.ground: Advice, not triggered. The CEO proposes standard commercial terms through the Investment Committee and no money beyond our share. If either changes, I withhold my support, and it comes to the Board first.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view in five cases.
(1) A 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, or an A350 Re-engine, goes on the record, and the 2050 grid shows a widebody row inside the caps. For the upgrade, that means no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column. For UltraFan WB, no more than $1.00B below hold. I would re-run both, but I do not expect either to pass.
(2) RR widebody share heads toward the 50% line, which triggers the franchise test.
(3) Delivered numbers put Joint Venture early-unit or durability costs above the top of my shared base ($4.3B), or a retrofit bill lands. I would hold buybacks first and bring any step beyond that to the Board before it arises.
(4) Evidence that the Joint Venture needs RR cash beyond the $4B share, or that our work and revenue share falls below our 36.5% narrowbody share. I would re-price the engine value we count and take it to the Board.
(5) A flying-hour shock that threatens cash breakeven.
cfo.memo:
Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing this round touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights, 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08, and his numbers. Hold is +32.37 (+32.38 at the Board's). The upgrade is -6.47 in every column against a $2B bill. UltraFan WB is -8.83, worst -9.00, against a $4B bill. With the $5B strain inside the rows, both lose more than their own bill in every column. I withhold my co-signature on each. Premium at hold: $0.

Capex: £0 of new development at hold. Either widebody item would add about £0.49bn a year.

One correction. Last round I said the Joint Venture roughly halves the ramp. It halves what we share, support and any retrofit, not the losses on our own 1,460 engines a year. Our base is about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn), held at the top; the worst case falls from about $10B to $7.5B (£5.5bn). The board carries no ramp line, so I report the range, not an actual.

The fold avoided $2.29B (about £1.7bn); the $1.71B write-off was non-cash. Our cash stays within the $4B share. No balance-sheet trigger stands. Buybacks give way first.

Now it is quality of cash: the net LTSA balance on the Joint Venture fleet, time on wing, and who pays for a fix in a Pratt & Whitney module. Plan on half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn, until the governance note settles it.

My record is thin on Joint Venture terms; this is inference. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (held, in service)
tests.threshold: A narrowbody engine must be ready by each selecting airframe's EIS. Joint Venture engine ready at formation + 6, or earlier where a folded Solo is further along (the date the bulletin shows). A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Formed 2035. Formation + 6 would be 2041; the bulletin shows ready 2036, inherited from the folded GTF2 (2030 + 6). Our folded Solo was 2030 + 7 = 2037.
- NGSA (launched 2030, EIS 2037): ready 2036, 1 year of margin. PASS. Fitted: RR NB share 24.1% from 2037.
- fps (launched 2030, 10-year ramp-up, EIS 2040): 4 years of margin. PASS. Share 36.5% from 2040.
The engine is ready and in service, so no narrowbody readiness test applies to this round's orders, as the Board says. Both narrowbody fields are hold-only.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan WB, if launched (option C, not recommended)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB ready at launch + 6. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. It must be ready by that Re-engine's EIS (Re-engine EIS = launch + 5). A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Launched 2045, ready 2051.
- S1: no Re-engine on the record, so it never counts.
- S2 and S3: a Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050. UltraFan WB is ready in 2051, one year late. RR WB share in 2050 stays 55.2%.
- 2050 round: a launch then is ready in 2056, six years after a 2045 Re-engine's EIS.
This is ADVICE on an order I do not recommend. It is not a veto. At hold there is nothing to fail.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the earlier ready date the bulletin shows, here 2036). No new programme date, nothing on Re-engines or airframer dates, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the record.
tests.numbers:
Judged on the CEO's draft; I re-check the final text at step 4.
- 'The Joint Venture ... formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies': on the public record (formed 2035, ready 2036, fitted on NGSA and fps). Clean.
- No date for any new programme. The upgrade would count from 2048, and UltraFan WB would be ready no earlier than 2051. Neither is ordered or named.
- Nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates.
- No Joint Venture terms: it does not describe the configuration, design authority or work share.
- 'Trent time on wing keeps improving' and 'we fix the fleet first and anything new waits': no date. Clean.
Caution for step 4: no retrofit, durability-kit or growth-engine date in public, and no claim that an UltraFan-core engine sits in the Joint Venture.

tests.name: Support before EIS (and support at volume)
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint). Any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit needs a support plan through partner shops before EIS (inference).
tests.numbers:
There is no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit this round, and both EIS are past (NGSA 2037, fps 2040). So no support-before-EIS test applies.

STATUS FOR THE COMMITTEE (internal; inference; the board does not track it):
- The joint support agreement went into the 2035-36 formation documents.
- The network is our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service narrowbody shops.
- Narrowbody work goes only to high-performing suppliers.
- I claim no signature or shop count the record cannot show.

VOLUME (brief's year table):
- 1,460 RR-share NB engines a year from 2040, beside 188 WB.
- About 10,233 delivered by end-2044, 17,533 by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050.
- P&W's public term is 'one engine, GTF2' at an equal 36.5% share. If so, the joint network supports about 2,920 engines a year, about 20,466 by end-2044 (inference).

IS ANYTHING SHORT? The board shows no constraint, and the brief reports none.
Watch items (advice):
(1) life-limited-part and hot-section spares. P&W holds design authority and reviews its pacing parts weekly, so it controls them;
(2) partner-shop induction slots ahead of the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts;
(3) spare engines for severe-environment operators.

tests.name: In-service durability (report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee)
tests.threshold: Mature in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, support able to intervene early. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new moves (attr.). The board does not model durability.
tests.numbers:
WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS:
- In service on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040.
- P&W's pre-EIS gates for GTF2: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life.
- The engine was ready in 2036 with no slip.
- No in-service event appears on the public record.
I claim no test or in-service data the record cannot show.

HOT SECTION EXPOSURE:
- P&W is still inserting its Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet.
- The Joint Venture engine is GTF2, with P&W's core under P&W design authority.
- Whether GTF2 carries that exposure is not on the record, and we cannot see it without P&W's data. That is the governance gap: an equal share of risk and investment, without design authority over the hot section.

ASK FOR THE NOTE:
- access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement;
- life-limited parts declared at full life.

RETROFIT PLAN IF IT BITES (the Trent 1000 model):
(1) the Committee hears first, before anything is said in public;
(2) protect the fleet: inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool;
(3) the design authority (P&W, for gear and core) issues the kit, inserted at shop visit through the joint partner shops. The Board's precedent is fleet retrofit within two years;
(4) the date of anything new moves;
(5) the cost split is McCabe's number and the note's.
Shop visits: I use my 1,100-1,200 a year (midterm, widebody), not 1,400-1,500.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project (Joint Venture) beside a widebody project (UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade) carries a one-off $5B strain whenever both are on record, whatever their dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference; seat and company rule).
tests.numbers:
PLAN A (all hold): strain $0. Control's strain line is met. PASS.

PLAN B (upgrade):
- It runs 2045-48 beside a ramped Joint Venture fleet.
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and cannot be cancelled, so the $5B is permanent.
- Against hold: -6.47 in every column; -1.47 without the strain.

PLAN C (UltraFan WB):
- It runs 2045-51.
- Strain $5B. Against hold: -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02; -4.00 / -3.27 / -3.02 without the strain.

RED LINES:
- No UltraFan is in development, so the upgrade rule is not engaged.
- The Solo folded in 2035, so the UltraFan WB-beside-Solo rule is not engaged.
- Neither B nor C breaches a hard rule I enforce. Each breaks Control's strain line and is a Board would-veto.
The support case changes neither verdict. The upgrade uses the existing Trent network. UltraFan WB would need a support build for a Re-engine that is not on the record.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is 'not applicable' unless the brief reports a constraint. Flag the narrowbody ramp's need for partner MRO and high-performing suppliers, as advice.
tests.numbers:
ENGINES A YEAR:
- 1,460 NB plus 188 WB = 1,648 a year from 2042, against 197 in 2026 (8.4x).
- NB: 965 / 978 / 990 in 2037-39, then 1,460 from 2040.
- WB: 197 to 2041, then 188.
- The same in every column at hold.

The brief reports no constraint. ADVICE: concentrate supply on high-performing suppliers (GBP 685m of GBP 2.5bn in 2023), and add partner-shop capacity ahead of the narrowbody shop-visit wave.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
HOLD:
- 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050, in S1, S2 and S3.
- The GEnx upgrade counts from 2042.
- Worst year 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line. The franchise test is not triggered.

OPTIONS:
- Upgrade: 60.0% in 2050.
- UltraFan WB: 55.2%, because it is late.

S2 EXPOSURE: Airbus WB airframe share is 41.2% / 40.2% / 41.2% in 2050. We power the A350 alone. In S2 a re-engined 787 without UltraFan would also press our Trent 1000 slot after 2050. That is not on the board and is qualitative.

DEFENCE: the Trent time-on-wing work inside the existing budget, as an other move:
- longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000;
- life extension for life-limited parts;
- Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.
No programme, no strain.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: A cancelled, idle or folded UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. A qualitative note; grid values are never adjusted for it (inference).
tests.numbers:
The Solo folded in 2035 onto GTF2's frozen test plan, so UltraFan technology did not go into the Joint Venture configuration.
- It stays RR's and feeds Trent time on wing: a 2-way flow.
- That is also how our technology is protected under P&W's 'risk and investment, not technology' terms (inference).
- On the record we hold no module design authority in the Joint Venture engine. What we bring there is risk, investment and the support network.
- RX-0072 ('we are actually bringing a technology') applies to any later engine under our own design authority, and the governance note should say so plainly.
- The IAE lesson is alignment between partners (R-0318).
Qualitative; the grid is unchanged.

vetoes.plan: The CEO's lean: every field at hold (`ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`)
vetoes.ground:
NONE INVOKED.
- Maturity: no maturity is compressed. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps 2040.
- Early date: the draft discloses none.
- Support: no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is ordered, so the support ground cannot arise.
TEST FAILS against the plan: none. BINDING VETOES: none.

vetoes.plan: RESERVED FOR STEP 4: the final public statement, the public other moves and the rationale
vetoes.ground:
Civil veto. It is binding under the team rule if triggered, and it rests on attributed turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). Grounds:
(a) Any public date for a new programme earlier than launch plus development years (UltraFan WB 2051 if launched in 2045; the upgrade counting before 2048). Also any Joint Venture date other than the record's 2036, and any retrofit, durability-kit or growth-engine date.
(b) A statement, other move or rationale that counts on an engine before its ready year. For example: an UltraFan-core Joint Venture engine in service, or UltraFan WB counting on a 2050 Re-engine.
(c) Any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit without a partner-shop support plan before EIS. No such order is open this round.

vetoes.plan: `t1000_upgrade: launch` or `ultrafan_wb: launch` (options B and C)
vetoes.ground:
Neither is a Civil ground, and neither breaches a hard rule I enforce: no UltraFan is in development, and the Solo folded in 2035.
ADVICE, NOT BINDING:
- Each carries a permanent $5B of strain and breaks Control's strain line.
- Upgrade: -6.47 in every column, more than its $2B bill; -1.47 without the strain.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02, more than its $4B bill. It also fails Ready by EIS (2051 against a 2045 Re-engine's 2050 EIS).
The Board would veto both. Hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I WOULD INVOKE THE BINDING CIVIL VETO AT STEP 4 IF:
- the final statement or a public other move gives a date for a new programme, a retrofit or a growth engine;
- it gives any Joint Venture date other than the record's;
- it gives any Re-engine or airframer date;
- it claims an UltraFan-core engine sits in the Joint Venture.

I WOULD PUT THE FLEET BEFORE ANY NEW ITEM, AND TELL THE COMMITTEE FIRST, IF:
- P&W's hot-section or life-limited-part data shows that GTF2 carries the GTF Hot Section exposure; or
- an in-service durability event appears on NGSA or fps.
The retrofit would then run through the joint partner shops before anything new.

I WOULD RE-TEST THE WIDEBODY ITEMS IN 2050 ONLY IF:
- a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S2, S3); or
- RR widebody share heads toward 50%.
Even then:
- an upgrade launched in 2050 counts from 2053 and still carries the $5B;
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056.
I would back either only if the grid shows it at or above hold, or within a declared premium under the caps.

I WOULD BACK THE UPGRADE ON THE SEAT'S USUAL LEAN only if its row beat hold. Today it is -6.47, and -1.47 even without the strain. Named airline durability results on the Joint Venture engine would strengthen the fleet case.
ops.memo:
The fleet comes first. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036: on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040, our share 1,460 engines a year, 10,233 by end-2044. No narrowbody readiness test applies, and no Civil ground arises at hold.

Durability: the record shows no in-service event, and I claim nothing beyond it. The gap is design authority. P&W keeps the gear and the core, and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. We carry half the risk without the hot-section data. The governance note must give us that data, life-limited parts at full declared life, and a fleet-first retrofit rule: Committee first, kit through the joint partner shops, as with the Trent 1000.

Support: the joint agreement and Singapore-model partner shops carry the volume. No shortfall on the board. Spares and shop slots before the first shop-visit wave are my watch items.

Technology: UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. On the record we hold no design authority here; we bring risk, investment and support. The note should say so.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column. I'd normally push the upgrade with no UltraFan in development, but it's -6.47, and -1.47 without the strain. UltraFan WB would be ready 2051, a year after a 2045 Re-engine's EIS. Hold both; time on wing inside budget does the job.

Statement clean; every field at hold.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

other_moves.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance and alignment note to the Board before the 2050 round
other_moves.detail:
Owners: Watson and McCabe. It covers:
(1) Design authority. Plainly: on the record P&W keeps the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology as its modules under its design authority. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan technology stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] applies to any later engine under our own design authority, which would come to the Board as a new programme with its own full test plan.
(3) Data. We ask for access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement, since we carry an equal share of the risk.
(4) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Until that is settled we plan on half of a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; the worst case is about £2.2bn.
(5) Work share and revenue. Both should be reflected at 36.5% each, matching the equal narrowbody shares. If our content per engine is below half, the board's engine value overstates our cash, and McCabe re-prices it.
(6) The joint support network.
(7) Cash stays within our $4B share. Nothing more goes in without the Board.
The IAE lesson is not to drift out of alignment [R-0318]. Doctrine and McCabe's and Watson's inference: my own record is Low on Joint Venture terms.

other_moves.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.

other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

other_moves.move: The 2050 test, set in advance
other_moves.detail:
This is the last round. Both widebody rows come to the ExCo only if a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record this round, or if RR widebody share heads toward 50%. Both carry the permanent $5B of strain.
- Upgrade launched in 2050: it counts from 2053. To pass the worst-case test it must be no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column, which needs about +$5B of engine value against about +0.53 today. Within the $3B cap it needs about +$4B.
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050: it is ready in 2056. It qualifies only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, on the record. It must be within $1.00B of hold, which needs about +$8B of engine value against +0.73 to +0.98 today.
I expect hold. The narrowbody fields stay at hold.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. We said that when we commit, we deliver. We did. Now the fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the partner-shop network. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year, and we will not launch for the sake of it. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
Every field is at hold:
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: hold`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
This is my framing proposal, unchanged. Both memos recommend the same orders, and there are no Board items. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only) is right because no airframe can use a new widebody engine in time [RX-0058].

GRID (brief rows, S1-S3)
- "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61. Components: engine value +38.07, R&D -4.00, write-offs -1.71. It is the best plan in every column.
- Weights S1-S3: 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08. McCabe confirmed them.
  - S1 (rivals hold): neither airframer has signalled a Re-engine. Boeing puts 787 customers and Charleston capacity first; Airbus runs "one well-prepared programme at a time".
  - S2 (787 Re-engine): 0.12. Boeing is the likelier mover, with fps in service since 2040.
  - S3 (both Re-engines): 0.08.
- Expected PV: +32.37 at my weights, +32.38 at the Board's illustration (0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10), +32.40 at McCabe's stress weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20). Worst column +32.35. Premium $0.

ROWS STRUCK, as gain over hold
- "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade": -6.47 in every column, so -6.47 under any weights. Worst -6.47 against its own $2B bill. Without the $5B strain it is still -1.47: about +0.53 of engine value against $2B.
  - It fails the four-part gate on business model [RX-0030].
  - The franchise test is not triggered: widebody share is 55.2%, above the line.
